The people of the city gathered around him, young and old, and they began looking at him and saying, "By God, this youth is not from the people of this city; we have never seen him in it, and we do not know him." Tamlikha did not know what to say to them, while he heard what they were saying. When the people of the city had gathered around him, he trembled, fell silent, and did not speak. Had he said that he was from the people of the city, he would not have been believed. He was certain that his father and brothers were in the city, and that his lineage was among the city's notables, and that they would come to him when they heard. And he was certain that yesterday evening he had known many of its people, and that today he knew none of them.

While he was standing like one bewildered, waiting for some of his family to come to him, his father or some of his brothers, to free him from their hands, they suddenly seized him and took him to the two leaders and administrators of the city who managed its affairs. They were two righteous men, one named Armus (Arnus) and the other named Asṭiyūs (Ustiyus). When they took him to them, Tamlikha thought he was being taken to Daqyanus the tyrant, their king, from whom they had fled. He began to look right and left. The people mocked him as they mock a madman or one bewildered. Tamlikha wept, then raised his head to heaven and to God, Mighty and Majestic, and said: "O God, Lord of the heavens and the earth, pour upon me today patience, and cause a spirit from You to enter me, by which You may strengthen me before this tyrant." He wept and said to himself: "They have separated me from my brothers! Would that they knew what I have suffered and where I am being taken. If only they knew, they would come, and we would all stand before this tyrant together. For we had pledged to one another that we would not disbelieve in God, nor associate anything with Him, nor worship the idols besides God, [and so] [[In the manuscript: "together, we must."]] they have separated me from them, and I will never see them nor will they see me. We had pledged not to be separated in life or in death. Would that I knew what he will do to me! Will he kill me or not?"

This is what Tamlikha related to his companions about himself, until he was brought to the two righteous men, Armus and Asṭiyūs. When Tamlikha saw that he had not been taken to Daqyanus, he came to himself and his weeping subsided. Armus and Asṭiyūs took the silver coins, looked at them, and were amazed. Then one of them said, "Where is the treasure you found, young man? This silver testifies against you that you found a treasure." Tamlikha said to them: "I have found no treasure. But this silver is the silver of my fathers, and the engraving and striking of this city. But by God, I do not know what my condition is, nor what I should say to you." One of them said, "Who are you?" He said to him: "As for what I see, I used to think I was from the people of the town." They said to him: "Who is your father, and who knows you there?" He told them his father's name, but they could not find anyone who knew him, nor his father. One of them said to him: "You are a liar, and you do not tell us the truth." He did not know what to say to them, except that he lowered his gaze to the ground. Some of those around him said, "This man is mad." Others said, "He is not mad, but he is deliberately feigning foolishness so that he may escape from you."

One of them said to him, looking at him intently: "Do you think we will send you away and believe you, that this is the wealth of your father, and that the striking and engraving of this silver is more than three hundred years old, while you are a young boy who thinks he can deceive us and mock us? We are the notables, as you see, and the rulers of its affairs, and the treasuries of this town are in our hands, and we have no silver coin of this striking, neither dirham nor dinar! I think I will order that you be tortured severely, and then bind you until you confess to this treasure you have found."

When he said that to him, Tamlikha said: "Tell me about something I will ask you, and if you do, you will believe what I have." They said to him: "Ask. We will not conceal anything from you." He said: "What has become of King Daqyanus?" They said to him: "We do not know of any king called Daqyanus on the face of the earth. He was only a king who died a long time ago, a very long age, and many centuries have passed since then." Tamlikha said to them: "By God, no one among mankind will believe what I say! We were youths, and the king forced us to worship idols and to sacrifice to the tyrants, so we fled from him yesterday evening and slept. When we awoke, I went out to buy food for my companions and to spy on the news, and behold, I am as you see. Come with me to the cave in the mountain of Yanjalus, and I will show you my companions."

When Armus heard what Tamlikha said, he said: "O people, perhaps this is one of God's signs, Mighty and Majestic, which He has made for you through this youth. Come with us, and let him show us his companions as he said." Armus and Asṭiyūs set out with them, and the people of the city, young and old, set out with the two of them toward the Companions of the Cave, looking at them.

When the youths, the Companions of the Cave, saw that Tamlikha had been delayed in bringing them their food and drink beyond the usual time, they thought he had been seized and taken to their king Daqyanus, from whom they had fled. While they were thinking this and fearing, they suddenly heard voices and the noise of horses ascending toward them. They thought they were the messengers of Daqyanus the tyrant, and that he had sent for them so that they might be brought. When they heard that, they stood for prayer, greeted one another, and said: "Come, let us go to our brother Tamlikha, for he is now before the tyrant Daqyanus, waiting for us to come to him." While they were saying this, sitting among the interior of the cave, they saw only Armus and his companions standing at the entrance of the cave. Tamlikha went ahead of them, entered upon them, weeping. When they saw him weeping, they wept with him and asked him about his condition. He told them his story and related all the news to them. Then they understood that they had been asleep by God's command all that time, and that they had only been awakened to be a sign for the people and a confirmation of the Resurrection, and so that they would know that ﴿the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it﴾.

Then Armus entered after Tamlikha and saw a copper chest sealed with a silver seal. He stood at the entrance of the cave, then called men of the city's notables, and the chest was opened in their presence. They found in it two sheets of lead, on which was written: "Maksalmina, Majsalmina, Tamlikha, Marṭulus, Kasṭūnus, Bīyusris, Takriyus and Baṭīnūs [[It is noted that the number counted is eight, not seven.]] were youths who fled from their king Daqyanus the tyrant, fearing that he would tempt them away from their religion. They entered this cave, and when their location was reported, he ordered the cave to be sealed with stones over them. We have written their matter and their story so that whoever comes after them and finds them may know it."

When they saw this, they were amazed, praised God who had shown them a sign of the Resurrection in them, and then they raised their voices in praise and glorification of God. Then they entered upon the youths of the cave and found them sitting among its interior, with radiant faces, and their garments had not decayed. Armus and his companions fell down in prostration and praised God who had shown them one of His signs. Then they spoke to one another, and the youths informed them of what they had suffered from their king Daqyanus.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 18, verse 9–16 (part 3 of 3):

Then Armus and his companions sent a messenger to their righteous king, Tidosius, saying: "Hasten, perhaps you will look upon one of the signs of God which God has placed upon your kingdom, and made a sign for the worlds, so that it may be a light, a radiance, and a confirmation of the Resurrection. So hasten to the youths whom God the Exalted has raised up, though He had caused them to die more than three hundred years earlier."

When the news reached the king, he rose from the seat on which he was sitting, his reason returned to him, his concern left him, and he turned to God the Mighty and Majestic, and said: "I praise You, Allah, Lord of the heavens and the earth, and I worship You and glorify You. You have shown favour to me and had mercy on me with Your mercy, and You did not extinguish the light which You had placed for my forefathers and for the righteous servant, King Tesetius."

When the people of the city were informed, they mounted and set out until they came to the city of Daqyanus. The people of the city met them and went with him until they ascended towards the cave and came to it. When Tidosius saw the youths, they rejoiced at him and fell down prostrate on their faces. Tidosius stood before them, then embraced them and wept, while they sat before him on the ground, glorifying God the Mighty and Majestic and praising Him. Then the youths said to Tidosius: "We commit you to God, and we send you our greetings, and may God preserve you and preserve your kingdom, and we seek refuge with God from the evil of the jinn and mankind."

While the king was standing, they returned to their resting places, lay down, and God took their souls. The king came to them, placed his garments upon them, and ordered that a coffin of gold be made for each man of them. When evening came and he slept, they came to him in a dream and said: "We were not created from gold or silver, but we were created from earth, and to earth we shall return. So leave us as we were in the cave, upon the earth, until God the Mighty and Majestic raises us from it." The king then ordered a coffin of teak, and they were placed in it. God veiled them with awe when they had left them, so that no one could enter upon them. The king ordered that a mosque be built at the entrance of the cave in which to pray, and he established for them a great festival, and ordered that it be held every year.

It is also said: when they came to the entrance of the cave, Tamlikha said: "Leave me until I enter upon my companions and give them good news, for if they see you with me, you will terrify them." He entered and gave them good news, and God took his soul and their souls, and their place was hidden from them, so they could not find it. This is the account of the companions of the Cave.

It is said that the Prophet of God, Muhammad (ﷺ), asked his Lord to show him them, and He said: "You will not see them in the life of this world, but send to them four of your best companions to convey your message to them and call them to belief in you."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Jibril (peace be upon him): "How shall I send them?" He said: "Spread a cloak for them, and seat Abu Bakr on one of its corners, Umar on the second, Ali on the third, and Abu Dharr on the fourth; then call the gentle wind that was subjected to Sulayman ibn Dawud (peace be upon them both), for God has commanded it to obey you."

The Prophet (ﷺ) did as he was commanded, and the wind carried them until it brought them to the entrance of the cave. When they drew near the entrance, they pulled a stone from it. The dog rose when it saw the light, growled and charged at them, but when it saw them it shook its head, wagged its tail, and gestured with its head that they should enter. They entered the cave and said: "Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings." God returned their souls to them, and they all rose and said: "Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings."

They said: "The Prophet of God, Muhammad son of Abdullah (ﷺ), sends you his greetings." They said: "Upon Muhammad, Messenger of God, be peace for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, and upon you for what you have conveyed." Then they all sat down talking together, and they believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) and accepted the religion of Islam, and said: "Convey to Muhammad our greetings." Then they lay down in their resting places and returned to their sleep until the end of time, at the emergence of the Mahdi.

It is said that the Mahdi will greet them, and God the Mighty and Majestic will revive them; then they will return to their sleep and will not rise again until the Day of Resurrection.

Then each of them sat in his place, the wind carried them, and Jibril (peace be upon him) descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of what had happened [with them]. When they came to the Prophet (ﷺ), the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "How did you find them? And what did they answer?" They said: "O Messenger of God, we entered upon them and greeted them, and they all rose, returned the greeting, and we conveyed your message to them. They responded, turned in repentance, and bore witness that you are truly the Messenger of God, and they praised God the Mighty and Majestic for honouring them with your coming forth and the sending of Your messenger to them, and they send you greetings."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O God, do not separate me from my in-laws, my beloved ones and my brethren, forgive those who love me, love the people of my household and my kin, and love my companions." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/390, with slight variation.]] [67]

That is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: "When the youths sought refuge in the cave" — i.e., they came to it and gathered together — "the cave" being a cavern in a mountain called Yanjalus, and the name of the cave being Khaylam. "They said: Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and facilitate for us a right course in our affair" — i.e., make easy for us what we seek of Your pleasure. Ibn Abbas said: "a right course" means an exit from the cave in safety.

It is also said: "right judgement."

As for His words, "So We struck upon their ears" — this is among the eloquent expressions of the Qur'an, which the Arabs acknowledged as beyond their ability to match. Its meaning is: We put them to sleep, cast and imposed sleep upon them, as one says: "God struck so-and-so with paralysis," meaning He afflicted him with it and sent it upon him. It is also said that the meaning is: We veiled them from hearing and blocked the penetration of sound into their ears, and this is a description of the dead and the sleeping. Qutrub said: it is like the saying of the Arabs: "The ruler struck upon the hand of the subjects," when he prevents them from mischief and corruption, and "the master struck upon the hand of his licensed slave in trade," when he prevents him from disposing of it. Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, who was blind, said:

"And of the calamities, may you have no father, that I was made blind, the earth struck upon me with barriers."

"For a number of years" — i.e., counted; it is an adjective of "years." Al-'add is the verbal noun, and al-'adad is the counted noun, like al-naqs and al-naqd, al-khabt and al-habt. Abu Ubayda said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun.

"Then We raised them up" — meaning from their sleep — "that We might know which of the two parties was better at computing the time they had remained" — this was when the early Muslims disputed with the companions of the king, and the later Muslims who had embraced Islam, concerning the length of their stay in the cave when the companions of the cave had taken refuge. The early Muslims said: "They remained in their cave three hundred years and nine," and the later Muslims said: "Rather, they remained so-and-so long." The former said: "God knows best how long they remained," and that is His words: "Then We raised them up, that you might know which of the two parties [i.e., the factions] was more accurate and more exact in computing how long they had remained in the cave asleep, a term (amad)": a limit.

Mujahid said: "a number." Its accusative has two possibilities: one as explanation, and the second because of its governing "how long they had remained."

"We relate" — i.e., We recite and send down to you "their account" — i.e., the news of the companions of the cave — "in truth. Indeed, they were youths" — young men and lads — "who believed in their Lord," God judged them to be youths because they believed without intermediary for that. The people of language said: the head of youthfulness is faith. Al-Junayd said: youthfulness is restraint from harm, giving generously, and abandoning complaint. It is also said: youthfulness is two things: avoiding the forbidden and practising noble conduct. It is also said: the youth is one who does not claim before the deed nor praise himself after the deed. It is also said: the youth is not one who endures the whip; the youth is one who passes over the bridge. It is also said: the youth is not one who endures the knife; the youth is one who feeds the poor.

"And We increased them in guidance" — in faith, insight and certainty.

"And We strengthened their hearts" — We fortified them with patience, inspired them with that, and strengthened them with the light of faith, until they endured abandoning the abode of their people and separation from the ease of life in which they had been, and fled with their religion to the cave, when they stood before Daqyanus, and said, when he rebuked them for abandoning the worship of the idol: "Our Lord is Lord of the heavens and the earth; we shall never call upon any god besides Him. We would have uttered then an enormity." That is, if we called upon other than God. Ibn Abbas and Muqatil said: "injustice." Qatada said: "a lie." The root of shatat and ishtat is exceeding the measure and excess.

"These, our people, have taken gods besides Him" — i.e., besides God — "idols they worship besides God. Why do they not bring a clear authority concerning them?" — with a manifest proof. "Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God," claiming that He has a partner and a son?

Then some of them said to others: "And when you have withdrawn from them" — i.e., from your people — "and from what they worship except God," meaning: and you have withdrawn from their idols which they worship besides God. Thus it is in the codex of Abdullah: "and what they worship besides God."

"Then take refuge in the cave" — i.e., go to it. "Your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you of your affair a means of ease" — i.e., abundant sustenance. The word mirfaq means what a person relies upon for support, and it has two forms: mirfaq and marfaq.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 18, verses 9–16 (part 1 of 3)**

﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were among Our signs as a wonder?﴾ Its meaning: "Rather, do you think?" That is, did you suppose, O Muhammad, that the companions of the cave and al-Raqim were among Our signs a wonder? That is, they are not the most wondrous of Our signs, for what We created of the heavens and the earth and what is in them of marvels is more astonishing than them. The *kahf* (cave) is the cave in the mountain. The scholars differed concerning *al-Raqim*. [In the manuscript: "قال" (he said) appears here.] One view is what Ibn Jurayj narrated from Musa ibn Uqba, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Three men went out seeking provision for their families. While they were walking, [In the manuscript: "إذا" (when).] the sky overtook them, so they took shelter in a cave. A rock fell from the mountain and sealed the mouth of the cave, locking them in. One of them said: 'Recall which of you has done a good deed, so that perhaps Allah, by His mercy [In a marginal note of the manuscript: "ببركته" (by His blessing).] will have mercy on us.'

One of them said: 'I once did a good deed. I had workers who labored for me, and I hired each man for a known wage. One day a man came to me at midday, and I hired him on the same condition as his companions. He worked the rest of the day just as the others had worked the whole day. I saw it as my duty not to diminish for him what I had paid his companions, since he had exerted himself in his work. But one of them said: "Do you give this man what you gave me, when he has worked only half a day?" I said: "O servant of Allah, I have not deprived you of anything of your agreed wage. It is my wealth, and I dispose of it as I wish."

He became angry, left, and abandoned his wage. So I placed his due in a corner of the house for as long as Allah willed. Then a herd of cattle came to me, and I bought with it a young cow, which grew as Allah willed. After some time an elderly, weak man whom I did not recognize passed by me and said: "I have a right over you." He mentioned it until I recognized him. I said: "I was seeking you, and this is your right."

I presented them all to him, and he said: "O servant of Allah, do not mock me. If you do not give me charity, then give me my right." I said: "By Allah, I am not mocking you. They are your right, and I have no claim to any of them," and I gave them to him. O Allah, if I did that for Your sake, then relieve us of this.' The mountain split apart until they saw the light and could see.

The other said: 'I once did a good deed. I had surplus wealth, and the people were struck by hardship. A woman came to me seeking a favor. I said: "By Allah, it is not less than yourself." She refused me and left. She returned three times, and each time I said: "No, by Allah, it is not less than yourself." She refused me and left, and she told her husband. He said to her: "Give him yourself and relieve your dependents." She came back to me and implored me by Allah, but I refused her and said: "By Allah, it is not less than yourself." When she saw that, she gave herself to me. But when I uncovered her and was about to approach her, she trembled beneath me. I said to her: "What is wrong with you?" She said: "I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds." I said to her: "You feared Him in hardship, and I did not fear Him in ease!" So I left her and gave her what was due to her in return for what I had uncovered. O Allah, if I did that for Your sake, then relieve us of this.' It split open until they recognized one another and things became clear to them.

The other said: 'I once did a good deed. I had two elderly parents, and I had sheep. I used to feed my parents and give them drink, then return to my family. One day rain detained me until evening. I came to my family and took my milking vessel, milked my sheep, and left them standing, then went to my parents. I found them asleep. It was hard for me to wake them, and hard for me to leave my sheep. So I remained sitting, with the milking vessel in my hand, until dawn woke them, and I gave them drink. O Allah, if I did that for Your sake, then relieve us of this.' [In the manuscript, after this there is a mark of omission, but it does not appear in its photograph.] [65]

Al-Nu'man said: "It is as though I hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The rock said: "Enough," and Allah relieved them, and they came out.'" [66] [In the manuscript: Musnad Ahmad 4/275 and Majma' al-Zawa'id 8/140, with slight variation.]

Ibn Abbas said: *al-Raqim* is a valley between Ghatafan and Aylah, and it is the valley in which the companions of the cave were.

Ka'b said: it is their town. On this interpretation it derives from *raqmat al-wadi*, which is the place of water in it. The Arabs say: "Take the *raqma*, and leave the *dafa*." The two *dafatan* are the two sides of the valley.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: *al-Raqim* is a plate of iron, and it was said of lead, in which they wrote the names of the companions of the cave and their story, then placed it at the mouth of the cave. On this interpretation it means *al-marqum*, that is, the written. *Al-raqm* is the line and the sign, and *al-raqm* is writing.

Then He mentioned their story, saying: ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave﴾, that is, they returned and became. The scholars differed concerning their journey to the cave. Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar said: The people of the Gospel fell into disorder, great sins multiplied among them, and the kings tyrannized over them until they worshipped idols and sacrificed to false gods. Among them there remained remnants upholding the religion of the Messiah, Son of Mary (peace be upon him), holding fast to the worship and unity of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Among their kings who did this was a king of the Romans called Decius (Daqyanus), who had worshipped idols and sacrificed to false gods, and who killed whoever opposed him in this among those who adhered to the religion of the Messiah. He would stop in the towns of the Romans, and in no town where he stayed did he leave anyone without tempting them until they worshipped idols and sacrificed to false gods. Then he came to the city of the companions of the cave, which was Ephesus. When he arrived there, it grieved the people of faith, so they hid from him and fled in every direction. When Decius entered it, he had ordered that the people of faith be pursued and gathered for him. He appointed an enforcement force from among the unbelievers of the city, and they went hunting the people of faith in their homes and brought them out to Decius. He would bring them to the congregation place where he sacrificed to false gods, and he gave them the choice between death and worshipping idols and sacrificing to false gods. Some of them preferred life, and some refused to worship other than Allah, so they were killed.

When the people who were steadfast in faith in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, saw this, they began to surrender themselves to torment and death. They were killed and cut into pieces, and then the pieces of their bodies were hung on the city walls on all sides and at every one of its gates. The trial became severe for the people of faith: some of them professed (disbelief) and were spared, and some were crucified for their religion and killed.

When the youths saw this, they grieved greatly. They stood, prayed, fasted, and occupied themselves with supplication and glorification of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. They were among the nobles of the Romans, and they were eight men. They wept, humbled themselves, and began to say: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; we will never call upon any god besides Him; for we would have uttered an enormity﴾. ﴿Relieve Your servants of this trial, lift from them this affliction, and bestow favor upon Your servants who believed in You, until they proclaim Your worship.﴾

While they were in this state, the police came upon them. They had entered their place of prayer, and they found them prostrate on their faces, weeping and humbling themselves before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, asking Him to save them from Decius and his party. When those unbelievers saw them, they said: "What has kept you from the king's command? Come to him." Then they left them and reported their affair to Decius, saying: "Shall we gather everyone, and these youths of your household mock you and disobey your command?" When he heard that, they were brought to him with their eyes flowing with tears, their faces covered with dust. He said to them: "What prevented you from witnessing the sacrifice to the gods that are worshipped on earth, and from making yourselves like others? Choose either to sacrifice to our gods as the people sacrificed, or I will kill you." Then Maksalmina, who was the eldest of them, said: "Indeed we have a God whose majesty fills the heavens and the earth. ﴿We will never call upon any god besides Him, ever.﴾ We will never acknowledge what you call us to, ever. Rather, we worship Allah, our Lord, and to Him belong praise, glorification, and exaltation from ourselves, sincerely. Him we worship, and from Him we seek deliverance and good. As for the false gods and their worship, we will never worship them, ever. So do with us whatever you will." Then the companions of Maksalmina said to Decius the same as he had said. When they said that, he commanded that the garments of their great men be stripped from them. Then he said: "As for you, since you have done this, I will postpone you, and I will be free for you, and I will carry out for you what I promised you of punishment. What prevents me from hastening that for you is only that I see you as young men, recently grown, and I do not wish to destroy you until I set for you a term in which you may remember and reconsider your minds."

Then he commanded that the ornaments of gold and silver which were on them be removed, and he ordered them to be taken out from his presence. Decius went to a city other than their own, near them, for some of his affairs. When the youths saw that Decius had left their city, they hastened to act, and they feared that if he returned to their city he would mention them. So they conspired among themselves that each man should take provision from his father's house, give it in charity, and take the rest as provision. Then they would go to a cave near the city on a mountain called Yanjalus, where they would remain and worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic, until Decius came, and they would stand before him, and he would do with them what he willed.

When they said this to one another, each youth went to his father's house and took provision, and they gave it in charity, and they departed with what remained of their provision. A dog they had followed them until they came to that cave in that mountain, and they stayed there.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: They passed by a dog, which barked at them, so they drove it away. It returned, and they did this several times. Then the dog said to them: "What do you want from me? You do not fear my response. I love the beloved ones of Allah, so sleep, and I will guard you."

Ibn Abbas said: They fled at night from Decius ibn Jalanus, when he invited them to worship idols. They were seven, and they passed by a shepherd who had a dog, and he was of their religion. They went out of the town and took refuge in the cave, which was near the town. They remained in it with no occupation except prayer, glorification, magnification, and praise, seeking the face of Allah, Exalted. They entrusted their provision to one of them called Tamlikha, who was in charge of their food, buying their provisions from the city secretly. He was among the most handsome and sturdy of them. Tamlikha used to do this: when he entered the town, he would take off his fine clothes and put on garments like those of the poor who ask for food, and then he would take a piece of paper and go to the city, buy food and drink, and listen and investigate to learn whether the people had mentioned his companions. Then he would return to his companions.

They remained in this state for as long as they remained. Then Decius the tyrant came to the city and ordered the notables to sacrifice to the false gods. The people of faith were frightened by this. Tamlikha was in the city buying food and drink for his companions, and he returned to them weeping, with a little food. He informed them that the tyrant Decius had entered the city and that they had been mentioned and sought along with the notables of the city, to be made to sacrifice to the false gods. When he informed them, they were terrified and fell prostrate, calling upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, humbling themselves and seeking refuge in Him from the trial.

Then Tamlikha said to them: "Lift up your heads, eat from the provision of Allah, and put your trust in your Creator."

They lifted their heads, their eyes flowing with tears out of grief and fear for themselves, and they ate from it, at sunset. Then they sat talking, studying, and mentioning one another. While they were in this state, ﴿Allah struck upon their ears in the cave﴾, and their dog stretched out its forelegs at the entrance of the cave. It was affected by what affected them, while they were believers, certain, and their provision was at their heads. When the next day came, Decius looked for them and sought them but did not find them. He said to some of them: "These youths who left have grieved me. They thought I was angry with them out of their ignorance of what they did not know about me. I would never have held anything against them in my heart, nor against any one of them, if they repented and worshipped my gods!" The notables of the city said to him: "You are not worthy to show mercy to a people who are wicked, rebellious, disobedient, persisting in their wrongdoing and disobedience. You had set a term for them, and if they had wished, they could have returned within that term, but they did not repent."

When they said that to him, he became exceedingly angry. Then he sent for their fathers and asked them about them, saying: "Tell me about your sons, the rebels who disobeyed me." They said to him: "As for us, we did not disobey you. Why would you kill us for the sake of a rebellious people who have taken our wealth and squandered it in the markets of the city, then went off and climbed a mountain called Yanjalus?" When they said that to him, he let them go, and he did not know what to do with the youths. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cast into his mind that he should command that the cave be sealed up over them. Allah willed to honor them, to make them a sign for a community that would succeed them, and to show them that ﴿the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will raise those in the graves﴾. [A reference to verse 70 of surah al-Hajj.]

Decius commanded that the cave be sealed up over them, and he said: "Leave them as they are in the cave, that they may die of thirst and hunger, and let their cave be their grave, which they chose." He thought they were awake and knew what was being done to them. But Allah had taken their souls in a sleep-like death, ﴿and their dog stretched out its forelegs at the threshold﴾, at the entrance of the cave, having been overtaken by what had overtaken them, ﴿turning them to the right and to the left﴾.

Then two believing men who were in the house of King Decius, concealing their faith, whose names were Bidarus and Ruttas, conspired to write the affair of the youths, their lineages, their names, and their story on a leaden tablet, which they placed in a copper chest, and then they placed the chest in the building. They said: "Perhaps Allah will reveal these youths to a people of believers before the Day of Resurrection, so that whoever opens it will know their story when he reads this book." They did so, then built over it. Decius remained for as long as he remained, then died, along with his people, and many generations passed, and kings succeeded kings.

Ubayd ibn Umayr said: The companions of the cave were youths adorned with torques, with bracelets, and with forelocks. With them was their hunting dog. They went out to a great festival of theirs in pomp and procession, and they took out with them the gods they worshipped besides Allah. Allah had cast faith into the hearts of the youths, and one of them was the minister of the king. They believed, and each one of them concealed his faith from his companion. They said to themselves, without any revealing it to the others: "We will leave among these people, so that no punishment for their crime will befall us." One youth went out until he reached the shade of a tree and sat in it. Then another went out and saw him sitting alone, and he hoped that he was in the same condition, without revealing it, so he sat with him. Then the others went out and came and sat with the two of them. They gathered, and one of them said to the others: "What brought you together, when each of you is concealing his faith from his companion for fear for his own self?" Then they said: "Let each two of you go out and be alone, and then let each one of you reveal to his companion."

Two youths went out and stood apart, then spoke, and each of them told his companion his affair. They came back to their companions, joyful, and said: "We have agreed on one matter." They were all then upon faith, and there was a cave in the mountain near them. One of them said to the others: ﴿Take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread for you some of His mercy and will prepare for you a means of ease in your affair.﴾ They entered, with a hunting dog with them, and they slept ﴿for three hundred years and added nine﴾.

He said: Their people missed them and sought them, but Allah concealed their traces and their cave from them. When they did not return, one of them wrote on a tablet: "So-and-so and so-and-so, sons of our kings, we have lost them in such-and-such a month of such-and-such a year, in the kingdom of so-and-so son of so-and-so." They placed the tablet in the king's treasury and said: "This will certainly have some consequence." The king died, and generation after generation came.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: One of the disciples of Jesus, son of Mary (peace be upon him), came to the city of the companions of the cave and wanted to enter it. It was said to him: "On its gate is an idol; no one enters it without prostrating to it." He disliked entering it, so he went to a bathhouse near that city and stayed in it. He hired himself out to the bathhouse keeper and worked there.

The owner of the bathhouse saw blessing in his bathhouse, his provision flowed to him, and he began to tend to it. Some youths from the city attached themselves to him, and he would tell them of the news of the heavens, the news of the earth, and the news of the Hereafter, until they believed in him and affirmed him, and they were in the same state as him in good bearing. His condition with the owner of the bathhouse had been: "The night is mine; no one may come between me and the prayer." He remained on this until the son of the king came with a woman and entered the bathhouse with her. The disciple (al-Hawari) reproached him and said, "You are the son of the king, and you enter with this one?" He was ashamed and left, but then he returned another time, and the disciple said to him the same thing. He cursed him and rebuked him and did not turn away, until the two of them entered together and died together in the bathhouse.

The king was informed, and it was said to him, "The owner of the bathhouse has killed your son." They sought him but could not reach him, so he fled. The king said, "Who used to accompany him?" They named the youths, and they were sought, and they left the city. They passed by a companion of theirs who was in his field, and he was of the same faith as they were. They told him that they were being sought, so he set out with them, and with him was a dog, until night overtook them at the cave. They entered and said, "Let us spend the night here, and then in the morning, God willing, you will see your opinion." Then "We struck upon their ears" (﴿فَضَرَبْنَا عَلَى آذَانِهِمْ فِي الْكَهْفِ سِنِينَ عَدَدًا﴾).

The king went out with his companions following them, until they found that they had entered the cave. Whenever any man among them wished to enter, he was terrified, and no one could bring himself to enter. One speaker said, "Did you not say that if you had power over them, you would kill them?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then wall up the entrance of the cave over them and leave them within it to die of thirst and hunger." He did so.

Wahb said: He left them after he had sealed the entrance of the cave, for a time after time. Then a shepherd whom the rain overtook near the cave said, "If only I could open this cave and bring my sheep into it from the rain!" He kept working at it until it opened. And God returned their souls to them the next day, when they awoke.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Then a righteous man named Tiyadusis (Theodosius) ruled over the people of those lands. When he became king, he remained in his kingdom for thirty-eight years. People split into factions during his reign, and they were factions: some believed in God and knew that the Hour is true, and some denied it. This grieved the righteous king, and he wept to God, the Mighty and Majestic, and humbled himself before Him, and he grieved a great grief. When he saw the people of falsehood increasing and prevailing over the people of truth, and saying, "There is no life but the life of this world, and only spirits are resurrected, not bodies; as for the body, the earth consumes it," and when they forgot what was in the Book, Tiyadusis began to send for those whom he thought to be good and to be with him in the truth. But they went on denying the Hour, until they nearly turned people away from the truth and from the creed of the Disciples.

When the righteous king Tiyadusis saw this, he entered his house and locked it upon himself. He put on a hair shirt, placed ashes beneath him, and sat upon them. He persisted, night and day, for a time, humbling himself to God and weeping over what he saw among the people, saying: "O Lord, You see the disagreement of these people. Send to them someone who will make it clear to them." Then the Merciful, the Compassionate, who dislikes the destruction of His servants, willed to make manifest the Companions of the Cave, the youths, to clarify their matter to the people, to make them a sign from Him and a proof against them, so that they would know that ﴿the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it﴾, and that He would answer His righteous servant Tiyadusis, complete His favor upon him, not remove from him his kingdom or the faith He had given him, that he should worship God and associate nothing with Him, and that He should gather together the believers in his land.

God, the Mighty and Majestic, cast into the heart of a man from the people of that land where the cave was, whose name was Awlyas (Ulyas), that he should demolish the structure that was over the mouth of the cave, and build from it an enclosure for his sheep. He hired two workers, and they began to remove those stones and build with them that enclosure, until they removed what was over the mouth of the cave and opened the entrance of the cave for them. God, Exalted, veiled them from the people by terror. It is claimed that the bravest man who wished to look at them, when he came to the entrance of the cave, did not advance until he saw their dog before them at the entrance of the cave, asleep.

When they removed the stones and opened the entrance of the cave, God, Mighty and Majestic, by His power, greatness and dominion, the Giver of Life to the dead, permitted the youths to sit among the interior of the cave. They sat joyful, with radiant faces and content hearts. Some of them greeted others, as though they had awoken from the same hour in which they used to wake when they rose in the morning after a night in which they had slept. Then they stood for prayer and prayed as they used to do. No trace of anything they disliked could be seen on their faces, their skin, or their colors; they were just as they had been when they fell asleep. And they thought that their king, Daqyanus the tyrant, was still seeking them.

When they had finished their prayer, they said to Tamlikha, the keeper of their provisions: "Go to us, our brother. What have the people said about our matter yesterday evening before this tyrant, while they think we had fallen asleep as some of our sleeps were, and it seemed to them that we had slept as long as we used to sleep on the night in which we rose?" Then they questioned one another, and some said to others, ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ They said, ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day.﴾ They said, ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained.﴾

All of that was easy for them. Tamlikha said to them: "They have sought you and searched for you in the city, and he wants you to be brought to him today, so that you will be slaughtered for the idols, or he will kill you. Then let God do what He wills." Then Maksalmina said to them: "O my brothers, know that you will meet God. So do not disbelieve after your faith if he calls you tomorrow." Then they said to Tamlikha: "Go to the city and listen to what is being said [about us] [[From ʿArāʾis al-Majālis; in the manuscript: "for us."]] there today, and what we are mentioned for before Daqyanus. Be discreet, and do not let anyone notice us. Buy us food and bring it to us, for hunger has overtaken us, and add to the food you brought us, for it was little, and we have become hungry."

Tamlikha did as he used to do: he put on his clothes and took the garments in which he used to disguise himself. He took silver coins from their provisions which were with them, struck with the seal of Daqyanus, and they were like the thin coins of the quarter (dirham). Tamlikha went out, and when he passed by the entrance of the cave he saw stones removed from the entrance of the cave, and he wondered at them. Then he passed on and paid them no attention, until he reached the gate of the city, concealing himself and keeping away from the road, fearing that someone of its people would see him, recognize him, and go to Daqyanus. The righteous servant did not realize that Daqyanus and his people had perished three hundred years before that.

When Tamlikha saw the gate of the city, he raised his eyes and saw, above the top of the gate, a sign that belongs to the people of faith. When he saw it he was amazed and began to look at it while hiding. He looked to the right and the left, then left that gate and moved to another of its gates, and looked and saw the like of it. It began to seem to him that the city was not the one he knew. He saw many people, new ones whom he had not seen before. He went on walking, amazed, and it seemed to him that he was bewildered. Then he returned to the gate by which he had come, wondering at it and at himself, and saying: "Would that I knew! Is this yesterday evening? The Muslims used to conceal this sign and hide it, but today it is manifest. Perhaps I am dreaming," and then he realized that he was not asleep.

He took his cloak and put it over his head, then entered the city. He walked among its markets and heard many people swearing by the name of Jesus son of Mary. This increased his fear, and he saw that he was bewildered. He stood, leaning his back against a wall of the city's walls, saying to himself: "By God, I do not know what this is. Yesterday evening, no one on earth who mentioned Jesus son of Mary was left unkilled, and now I hear them, and everyone mentions the matter of Jesus without fear."

Then he said to himself: "Perhaps this city is not the city I know. I hear the speech of its people and do not know any of them. By God, I know of no city near our city!" He stood like one bewildered, not turning in any direction. Then he met a youth from the people of the city and said, "What is the name of this city, young man?" He said, "Ephesus (Dafsus)." Tamlikha said to himself: "Perhaps there is something of madness in me, or some matter has taken away my mind. By God, I have every right to hurry out of it before I am disgraced or some evil befalls me and I perish."

This is what Tamlikha related to his companions when their situation became clear to him. Then he came to himself and said: "By God, if I had hurried out of it before they noticed me, it would have been wiser for me." He approached those who sell food, took out the silver coins he had with him and gave them to a man among them, and said, "O servant of God, sell me food for this silver." The man took them, looked at the striking and engraving of the coins, and wondered at them. Then he threw them to a man among his companions, who looked at them. They began passing them from one man to another, marveling at them, and then they began whispering about him. He trembled greatly and began to shake, thinking they had noticed him and recognized him, and that they only wanted to take him to their king Daqyanus.

Other people began to come to him and recognize him. He said to them, trembling greatly: "Give me a moment; you have taken my silver, so hold on to it. As for your food, I have no need of it." They said, "Who are you, young man? What is your condition? By God, you have found a treasure from the treasures of the ancients, and you want to conceal it from us. Come with us and show it to us, and share it with us, and we will spare you what you have found. For if you do not do so, we will bring you to the sultan, and hand you over to him, and he will kill you."

When he heard their words, he was amazed in himself and said: "I have fallen into everything I feared." Then they said: "Young man, by God, you cannot conceal what has happened, and do not think that you will hide it from us." Tamlikha did not know what to say to them or how to answer them, and he trembled so that he could not tell them anything. When they saw that he did not speak, they took his cloak and put it around his neck, then began leading him through the streets of the city, bent over, until word of it reached those in the city. It was said: "A man has been seized who has a treasure." The people of the city gathered around him, young and old, and they began looking at him and saying, "By God, this youth is not from the people of this city; we have never seen him in it, and we do not know him." Tamlikha did not know what to say to them, while he heard what they were saying. When the people of the city had gathered around him, he trembled, fell silent, and did not speak. Had he said that he was from the people of the city, he would not have been believed. He was certain that his father and brothers were in the city, and that his lineage was among the city's notables, and that they would come to him when they heard. And he was certain that yesterday evening he had known many of its people, and that today he knew none of them.

While he was standing like one bewildered, waiting for some of his family to come to him, his father or some of his brothers, to free him from their hands, they suddenly seized him and took him to the two leaders and administrators of the city who managed its affairs. They were two righteous men, one named Armus (Arnus) and the other named Asṭiyūs (Ustiyus). When they took him to them, Tamlikha thought he was being taken to Daqyanus the tyrant, their king, from whom they had fled. He began to look right and left. The people mocked him as they mock a madman or one bewildered. Tamlikha wept, then raised his head to heaven and to God, Mighty and Majestic, and said: "O God, Lord of the heavens and the earth, pour upon me today patience, and cause a spirit from You to enter me, by which You may strengthen me before this tyrant." He wept and said to himself: "They have separated me from my brothers! Would that they knew what I have suffered and where I am being taken. If only they knew, they would come, and we would all stand before this tyrant together. For we had pledged to one another that we would not disbelieve in God, nor associate anything with Him, nor worship the idols besides God, [and so] [[In the manuscript: "together, we must."]] they have separated me from them, and I will never see them nor will they see me. We had pledged not to be separated in life or in death. Would that I knew what he will do to me! Will he kill me or not?"

This is what Tamlikha related to his companions about himself, until he was brought to the two righteous men, Armus and Asṭiyūs. When Tamlikha saw that he had not been taken to Daqyanus, he came to himself and his weeping subsided. Armus and Asṭiyūs took the silver coins, looked at them, and were amazed. Then one of them said, "Where is the treasure you found, young man? This silver testifies against you that you found a treasure." Tamlikha said to them: "I have found no treasure. But this silver is the silver of my fathers, and the engraving and striking of this city. But by God, I do not know what my condition is, nor what I should say to you." One of them said, "Who are you?" He said to him: "As for what I see, I used to think I was from the people of the town." They said to him: "Who is your father, and who knows you there?" He told them his father's name, but they could not find anyone who knew him, nor his father. One of them said to him: "You are a liar, and you do not tell us the truth." He did not know what to say to them, except that he lowered his gaze to the ground. Some of those around him said, "This man is mad." Others said, "He is not mad, but he is deliberately feigning foolishness so that he may escape from you."

One of them said to him, looking at him intently: "Do you think we will send you away and believe you, that this is the wealth of your father, and that the striking and engraving of this silver is more than three hundred years old, while you are a young boy who thinks he can deceive us and mock us? We are the notables, as you see, and the rulers of its affairs, and the treasuries of this town are in our hands, and we have no silver coin of this striking, neither dirham nor dinar! I think I will order that you be tortured severely, and then bind you until you confess to this treasure you have found."

When he said that to him, Tamlikha said: "Tell me about something I will ask you, and if you do, you will believe what I have." They said to him: "Ask. We will not conceal anything from you." He said: "What has become of King Daqyanus?" They said to him: "We do not know of any king called Daqyanus on the face of the earth. He was only a king who died a long time ago, a very long age, and many centuries have passed since then." Tamlikha said to them: "By God, no one among mankind will believe what I say! We were youths, and the king forced us to worship idols and to sacrifice to the tyrants, so we fled from him yesterday evening and slept. When we awoke, I went out to buy food for my companions and to spy on the news, and behold, I am as you see. Come with me to the cave in the mountain of Yanjalus, and I will show you my companions."

When Armus heard what Tamlikha said, he said: "O people, perhaps this is one of God's signs, Mighty and Majestic, which He has made for you through this youth. Come with us, and let him show us his companions as he said." Armus and Asṭiyūs set out with them, and the people of the city, young and old, set out with the two of them toward the Companions of the Cave, looking at them.

When the youths, the Companions of the Cave, saw that Tamlikha had been delayed in bringing them their food and drink beyond the usual time, they thought he had been seized and taken to their king Daqyanus, from whom they had fled. While they were thinking this and fearing, they suddenly heard voices and the noise of horses ascending toward them. They thought they were the messengers of Daqyanus the tyrant, and that he had sent for them so that they might be brought. When they heard that, they stood for prayer, greeted one another, and said: "Come, let us go to our brother Tamlikha, for he is now before the tyrant Daqyanus, waiting for us to come to him." While they were saying this, sitting among the interior of the cave, they saw only Armus and his companions standing at the entrance of the cave. Tamlikha went ahead of them, entered upon them, weeping. When they saw him weeping, they wept with him and asked him about his condition. He told them his story and related all the news to them. Then they understood that they had been asleep by God's command all that time, and that they had only been awakened to be a sign for the people and a confirmation of the Resurrection, and so that they would know that ﴿the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it﴾.

Then Armus entered after Tamlikha and saw a copper chest sealed with a silver seal. He stood at the entrance of the cave, then called men of the city's notables, and the chest was opened in their presence. They found in it two sheets of lead, on which was written: "Maksalmina, Majsalmina, Tamlikha, Marṭulus, Kasṭūnus, Bīyusris, Takriyus and Baṭīnūs [[It is noted that the number counted is eight, not seven.]] were youths who fled from their king Daqyanus the tyrant, fearing that he would tempt them away from their religion. They entered this cave, and when their location was reported, he ordered the cave to be sealed with stones over them. We have written their matter and their story so that whoever comes after them and finds them may know it."

When they saw this, they were amazed, praised God who had shown them a sign of the Resurrection in them, and then they raised their voices in praise and glorification of God. Then they entered upon the youths of the cave and found them sitting among its interior, with radiant faces, and their garments had not decayed. Armus and his companions fell down in prostration and praised God who had shown them one of His signs. Then they spoke to one another, and the youths informed them of what they had suffered from their king Daqyanus.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 18, verse 9–16 (part 3 of 3):

Then Armus and his companions sent a messenger to their righteous king, Tidosius, saying: "Hasten, perhaps you will look upon one of the signs of God which God has placed upon your kingdom, and made a sign for the worlds, so that it may be a light, a radiance, and a confirmation of the Resurrection. So hasten to the youths whom God the Exalted has raised up, though He had caused them to die more than three hundred years earlier."

When the news reached the king, he rose from the seat on which he was sitting, his reason returned to him, his concern left him, and he turned to God the Mighty and Majestic, and said: "I praise You, Allah, Lord of the heavens and the earth, and I worship You and glorify You. You have shown favour to me and had mercy on me with Your mercy, and You did not extinguish the light which You had placed for my forefathers and for the righteous servant, King Tesetius."

When the people of the city were informed, they mounted and set out until they came to the city of Daqyanus. The people of the city met them and went with him until they ascended towards the cave and came to it. When Tidosius saw the youths, they rejoiced at him and fell down prostrate on their faces. Tidosius stood before them, then embraced them and wept, while they sat before him on the ground, glorifying God the Mighty and Majestic and praising Him. Then the youths said to Tidosius: "We commit you to God, and we send you our greetings, and may God preserve you and preserve your kingdom, and we seek refuge with God from the evil of the jinn and mankind."

While the king was standing, they returned to their resting places, lay down, and God took their souls. The king came to them, placed his garments upon them, and ordered that a coffin of gold be made for each man of them. When evening came and he slept, they came to him in a dream and said: "We were not created from gold or silver, but we were created from earth, and to earth we shall return. So leave us as we were in the cave, upon the earth, until God the Mighty and Majestic raises us from it." The king then ordered a coffin of teak, and they were placed in it. God veiled them with awe when they had left them, so that no one could enter upon them. The king ordered that a mosque be built at the entrance of the cave in which to pray, and he established for them a great festival, and ordered that it be held every year.

It is also said: when they came to the entrance of the cave, Tamlikha said: "Leave me until I enter upon my companions and give them good news, for if they see you with me, you will terrify them." He entered and gave them good news, and God took his soul and their souls, and their place was hidden from them, so they could not find it. This is the account of the companions of the Cave.

It is said that the Prophet of God, Muhammad (ﷺ), asked his Lord to show him them, and He said: "You will not see them in the life of this world, but send to them four of your best companions to convey your message to them and call them to belief in you."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Jibril (peace be upon him): "How shall I send them?" He said: "Spread a cloak for them, and seat Abu Bakr on one of its corners, Umar on the second, Ali on the third, and Abu Dharr on the fourth; then call the gentle wind that was subjected to Sulayman ibn Dawud (peace be upon them both), for God has commanded it to obey you."

The Prophet (ﷺ) did as he was commanded, and the wind carried them until it brought them to the entrance of the cave. When they drew near the entrance, they pulled a stone from it. The dog rose when it saw the light, growled and charged at them, but when it saw them it shook its head, wagged its tail, and gestured with its head that they should enter. They entered the cave and said: "Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings." God returned their souls to them, and they all rose and said: "Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings."

They said: "The Prophet of God, Muhammad son of Abdullah (ﷺ), sends you his greetings." They said: "Upon Muhammad, Messenger of God, be peace for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, and upon you for what you have conveyed." Then they all sat down talking together, and they believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) and accepted the religion of Islam, and said: "Convey to Muhammad our greetings." Then they lay down in their resting places and returned to their sleep until the end of time, at the emergence of the Mahdi.

It is said that the Mahdi will greet them, and God the Mighty and Majestic will revive them; then they will return to their sleep and will not rise again until the Day of Resurrection.

Then each of them sat in his place, the wind carried them, and Jibril (peace be upon him) descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of what had happened [with them]. When they came to the Prophet (ﷺ), the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "How did you find them? And what did they answer?" They said: "O Messenger of God, we entered upon them and greeted them, and they all rose, returned the greeting, and we conveyed your message to them. They responded, turned in repentance, and bore witness that you are truly the Messenger of God, and they praised God the Mighty and Majestic for honouring them with your coming forth and the sending of Your messenger to them, and they send you greetings."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O God, do not separate me from my in-laws, my beloved ones and my brethren, forgive those who love me, love the people of my household and my kin, and love my companions." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/390, with slight variation.]] [67]

That is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: "When the youths sought refuge in the cave" — i.e., they came to it and gathered together — "the cave" being a cavern in a mountain called Yanjalus, and the name of the cave being Khaylam. "They said: Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and facilitate for us a right course in our affair" — i.e., make easy for us what we seek of Your pleasure. Ibn Abbas said: "a right course" means an exit from the cave in safety.

It is also said: "right judgement."

As for His words, "So We struck upon their ears" — this is among the eloquent expressions of the Qur'an, which the Arabs acknowledged as beyond their ability to match. Its meaning is: We put them to sleep, cast and imposed sleep upon them, as one says: "God struck so-and-so with paralysis," meaning He afflicted him with it and sent it upon him. It is also said that the meaning is: We veiled them from hearing and blocked the penetration of sound into their ears, and this is a description of the dead and the sleeping. Qutrub said: it is like the saying of the Arabs: "The ruler struck upon the hand of the subjects," when he prevents them from mischief and corruption, and "the master struck upon the hand of his licensed slave in trade," when he prevents him from disposing of it. Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, who was blind, said:

"And of the calamities, may you have no father, that I was made blind, the earth struck upon me with barriers."

"For a number of years" — i.e., counted; it is an adjective of "years." Al-'add is the verbal noun, and al-'adad is the counted noun, like al-naqs and al-naqd, al-khabt and al-habt. Abu Ubayda said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun.

"Then We raised them up" — meaning from their sleep — "that We might know which of the two parties was better at computing the time they had remained" — this was when the early Muslims disputed with the companions of the king, and the later Muslims who had embraced Islam, concerning the length of their stay in the cave when the companions of the cave had taken refuge. The early Muslims said: "They remained in their cave three hundred years and nine," and the later Muslims said: "Rather, they remained so-and-so long." The former said: "God knows best how long they remained," and that is His words: "Then We raised them up, that you might know which of the two parties [i.e., the factions] was more accurate and more exact in computing how long they had remained in the cave asleep, a term (amad)": a limit.

Mujahid said: "a number." Its accusative has two possibilities: one as explanation, and the second because of its governing "how long they had remained."

"We relate" — i.e., We recite and send down to you "their account" — i.e., the news of the companions of the cave — "in truth. Indeed, they were youths" — young men and lads — "who believed in their Lord," God judged them to be youths because they believed without intermediary for that. The people of language said: the head of youthfulness is faith. Al-Junayd said: youthfulness is restraint from harm, giving generously, and abandoning complaint. It is also said: youthfulness is two things: avoiding the forbidden and practising noble conduct. It is also said: the youth is one who does not claim before the deed nor praise himself after the deed. It is also said: the youth is not one who endures the whip; the youth is one who passes over the bridge. It is also said: the youth is not one who endures the knife; the youth is one who feeds the poor.

"And We increased them in guidance" — in faith, insight and certainty.

"And We strengthened their hearts" — We fortified them with patience, inspired them with that, and strengthened them with the light of faith, until they endured abandoning the abode of their people and separation from the ease of life in which they had been, and fled with their religion to the cave, when they stood before Daqyanus, and said, when he rebuked them for abandoning the worship of the idol: "Our Lord is Lord of the heavens and the earth; we shall never call upon any god besides Him. We would have uttered then an enormity." That is, if we called upon other than God. Ibn Abbas and Muqatil said: "injustice." Qatada said: "a lie." The root of shatat and ishtat is exceeding the measure and excess.

"These, our people, have taken gods besides Him" — i.e., besides God — "idols they worship besides God. Why do they not bring a clear authority concerning them?" — with a manifest proof. "Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God," claiming that He has a partner and a son?

Then some of them said to others: "And when you have withdrawn from them" — i.e., from your people — "and from what they worship except God," meaning: and you have withdrawn from their idols which they worship besides God. Thus it is in the codex of Abdullah: "and what they worship besides God."

"Then take refuge in the cave" — i.e., go to it. "Your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you of your affair a means of ease" — i.e., abundant sustenance. The word mirfaq means what a person relies upon for support, and it has two forms: mirfaq and marfaq.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 18, verses 9–16 (part 1 of 3)**

﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were among Our signs as a wonder?﴾ Its meaning: "Rather, do you think?" That is, did you suppose, O Muhammad, that the companions of the cave and al-Raqim were among Our signs a wonder? That is, they are not the most wondrous of Our signs, for what We created of the heavens and the earth and what is in them of marvels is more astonishing than them. The *kahf* (cave) is the cave in the mountain. The scholars differed concerning *al-Raqim*. [In the manuscript: "قال" (he said) appears here.] One view is what Ibn Jurayj narrated from Musa ibn Uqba, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Three men went out seeking provision for their families. While they were walking, [In the manuscript: "إذا" (when).] the sky overtook them, so they took shelter in a cave. A rock fell from the mountain and sealed the mouth of the cave, locking them in. One of them said: 'Recall which of you has done a good deed, so that perhaps Allah, by His mercy [In a marginal note of the manuscript: "ببركته" (by His blessing).] will have mercy on us.'

One of them said: 'I once did a good deed. I had workers who labored for me, and I hired each man for a known wage. One day a man came to me at midday, and I hired him on the same condition as his companions. He worked the rest of the day just as the others had worked the whole day. I saw it as my duty not to diminish for him what I had paid his companions, since he had exerted himself in his work. But one of them said: "Do you give this man what you gave me, when he has worked only half a day?" I said: "O servant of Allah, I have not deprived you of anything of your agreed wage. It is my wealth, and I dispose of it as I wish."

He became angry, left, and abandoned his wage. So I placed his due in a corner of the house for as long as Allah willed. Then a herd of cattle came to me, and I bought with it a young cow, which grew as Allah willed. After some time an elderly, weak man whom I did not recognize passed by me and said: "I have a right over you." He mentioned it until I recognized him. I said: "I was seeking you, and this is your right."

I presented them all to him, and he said: "O servant of Allah, do not mock me. If you do not give me charity, then give me my right." I said: "By Allah, I am not mocking you. They are your right, and I have no claim to any of them," and I gave them to him. O Allah, if I did that for Your sake, then relieve us of this.' The mountain split apart until they saw the light and could see.

The other said: 'I once did a good deed. I had surplus wealth, and the people were struck by hardship. A woman came to me seeking a favor. I said: "By Allah, it is not less than yourself." She refused me and left. She returned three times, and each time I said: "No, by Allah, it is not less than yourself." She refused me and left, and she told her husband. He said to her: "Give him yourself and relieve your dependents." She came back to me and implored me by Allah, but I refused her and said: "By Allah, it is not less than yourself." When she saw that, she gave herself to me. But when I uncovered her and was about to approach her, she trembled beneath me. I said to her: "What is wrong with you?" She said: "I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds." I said to her: "You feared Him in hardship, and I did not fear Him in ease!" So I left her and gave her what was due to her in return for what I had uncovered. O Allah, if I did that for Your sake, then relieve us of this.' It split open until they recognized one another and things became clear to them.

The other said: 'I once did a good deed. I had two elderly parents, and I had sheep. I used to feed my parents and give them drink, then return to my family. One day rain detained me until evening. I came to my family and took my milking vessel, milked my sheep, and left them standing, then went to my parents. I found them asleep. It was hard for me to wake them, and hard for me to leave my sheep. So I remained sitting, with the milking vessel in my hand, until dawn woke them, and I gave them drink. O Allah, if I did that for Your sake, then relieve us of this.' [In the manuscript, after this there is a mark of omission, but it does not appear in its photograph.] [65]

Al-Nu'man said: "It is as though I hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The rock said: "Enough," and Allah relieved them, and they came out.'" [66] [In the manuscript: Musnad Ahmad 4/275 and Majma' al-Zawa'id 8/140, with slight variation.]

Ibn Abbas said: *al-Raqim* is a valley between Ghatafan and Aylah, and it is the valley in which the companions of the cave were.

Ka'b said: it is their town. On this interpretation it derives from *raqmat al-wadi*, which is the place of water in it. The Arabs say: "Take the *raqma*, and leave the *dafa*." The two *dafatan* are the two sides of the valley.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: *al-Raqim* is a plate of iron, and it was said of lead, in which they wrote the names of the companions of the cave and their story, then placed it at the mouth of the cave. On this interpretation it means *al-marqum*, that is, the written. *Al-raqm* is the line and the sign, and *al-raqm* is writing.

Then He mentioned their story, saying: ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave﴾, that is, they returned and became. The scholars differed concerning their journey to the cave. Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar said: The people of the Gospel fell into disorder, great sins multiplied among them, and the kings tyrannized over them until they worshipped idols and sacrificed to false gods. Among them there remained remnants upholding the religion of the Messiah, Son of Mary (peace be upon him), holding fast to the worship and unity of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Among their kings who did this was a king of the Romans called Decius (Daqyanus), who had worshipped idols and sacrificed to false gods, and who killed whoever opposed him in this among those who adhered to the religion of the Messiah. He would stop in the towns of the Romans, and in no town where he stayed did he leave anyone without tempting them until they worshipped idols and sacrificed to false gods. Then he came to the city of the companions of the cave, which was Ephesus. When he arrived there, it grieved the people of faith, so they hid from him and fled in every direction. When Decius entered it, he had ordered that the people of faith be pursued and gathered for him. He appointed an enforcement force from among the unbelievers of the city, and they went hunting the people of faith in their homes and brought them out to Decius. He would bring them to the congregation place where he sacrificed to false gods, and he gave them the choice between death and worshipping idols and sacrificing to false gods. Some of them preferred life, and some refused to worship other than Allah, so they were killed.

When the people who were steadfast in faith in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, saw this, they began to surrender themselves to torment and death. They were killed and cut into pieces, and then the pieces of their bodies were hung on the city walls on all sides and at every one of its gates. The trial became severe for the people of faith: some of them professed (disbelief) and were spared, and some were crucified for their religion and killed.

When the youths saw this, they grieved greatly. They stood, prayed, fasted, and occupied themselves with supplication and glorification of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. They were among the nobles of the Romans, and they were eight men. They wept, humbled themselves, and began to say: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; we will never call upon any god besides Him; for we would have uttered an enormity﴾. ﴿Relieve Your servants of this trial, lift from them this affliction, and bestow favor upon Your servants who believed in You, until they proclaim Your worship.﴾

While they were in this state, the police came upon them. They had entered their place of prayer, and they found them prostrate on their faces, weeping and humbling themselves before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, asking Him to save them from Decius and his party. When those unbelievers saw them, they said: "What has kept you from the king's command? Come to him." Then they left them and reported their affair to Decius, saying: "Shall we gather everyone, and these youths of your household mock you and disobey your command?" When he heard that, they were brought to him with their eyes flowing with tears, their faces covered with dust. He said to them: "What prevented you from witnessing the sacrifice to the gods that are worshipped on earth, and from making yourselves like others? Choose either to sacrifice to our gods as the people sacrificed, or I will kill you." Then Maksalmina, who was the eldest of them, said: "Indeed we have a God whose majesty fills the heavens and the earth. ﴿We will never call upon any god besides Him, ever.﴾ We will never acknowledge what you call us to, ever. Rather, we worship Allah, our Lord, and to Him belong praise, glorification, and exaltation from ourselves, sincerely. Him we worship, and from Him we seek deliverance and good. As for the false gods and their worship, we will never worship them, ever. So do with us whatever you will." Then the companions of Maksalmina said to Decius the same as he had said. When they said that, he commanded that the garments of their great men be stripped from them. Then he said: "As for you, since you have done this, I will postpone you, and I will be free for you, and I will carry out for you what I promised you of punishment. What prevents me from hastening that for you is only that I see you as young men, recently grown, and I do not wish to destroy you until I set for you a term in which you may remember and reconsider your minds."

Then he commanded that the ornaments of gold and silver which were on them be removed, and he ordered them to be taken out from his presence. Decius went to a city other than their own, near them, for some of his affairs. When the youths saw that Decius had left their city, they hastened to act, and they feared that if he returned to their city he would mention them. So they conspired among themselves that each man should take provision from his father's house, give it in charity, and take the rest as provision. Then they would go to a cave near the city on a mountain called Yanjalus, where they would remain and worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic, until Decius came, and they would stand before him, and he would do with them what he willed.

When they said this to one another, each youth went to his father's house and took provision, and they gave it in charity, and they departed with what remained of their provision. A dog they had followed them until they came to that cave in that mountain, and they stayed there.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: They passed by a dog, which barked at them, so they drove it away. It returned, and they did this several times. Then the dog said to them: "What do you want from me? You do not fear my response. I love the beloved ones of Allah, so sleep, and I will guard you."

Ibn Abbas said: They fled at night from Decius ibn Jalanus, when he invited them to worship idols. They were seven, and they passed by a shepherd who had a dog, and he was of their religion. They went out of the town and took refuge in the cave, which was near the town. They remained in it with no occupation except prayer, glorification, magnification, and praise, seeking the face of Allah, Exalted.
