﴿And you would have been filled with terror from them﴾: fear. The people of Medina read *lamulli'ta* with doubling. It was also said: this was only from the loneliness of the place they were in. al-Kalbi said: because their eyes were open, like one awake who wants to speak, while they were asleep. It was also said: God restrained them with terror so that no one would see them. Saʿid ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "We fought with Muʿawiyah the battle of al-Mudayiq toward the Romans, and we passed by the cave in which were the People of the Cave. Muʿawiyah said: 'If only it were revealed to us about these people, so that we could look at them!' Ibn ʿAbbas said: 'That is not for you; God has restrained someone better than you.' He said: ﴿If you had looked upon them you would have turned away from them in flight, and you would have been filled with terror from them﴾." Then Muʿawiyah said: "I will not stop until I know their state." So he sent some men and said: "Go and look." They did so, but when they entered the cave God sent a wind upon them that drove them out, and they could not look at them because of the terror.

﴿And thus We raised them up﴾: that is, just as We put them to sleep in the cave and prevented anyone from reaching them, and preserved their bodies from decay over the length of time, and their clothes from mould over the passing of days, by Our power. ﴿Thus We raised them up﴾ from that sleep which resembles death, ﴿that they might question one another﴾: that they might speak and ask one another. ﴿A speaker among them said﴾: that is, their leader, Maksilmina: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ For they were startled at their own long sleep. It is also said: what troubled them was the prayers they had missed, so they said that. ﴿They said: We have remained a day﴾, for they had entered the cave in the early morning; when they saw the sun they said ﴿or part of a day﴾, guarding against lying, since some of the sun's light still remained. It is also said: it was after the sun had passed its zenith. When they looked at their hair and nails, they were certain that their stay was more than a day or part of a day, and so ﴿they said: Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾. It is also said: when their leader heard the disagreement among them, he said that.

﴿So send one of you﴾, that is, Tamlikha, ﴿with this silver of yours to the city﴾. *Al-wariq* is silver, whether minted or unminted. The evidence for this is that ʿUrfajah ibn Asʿad had his nose struck off on the day of al-Kilab, so he made a nose of silver, which then stank upon him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to make a nose of gold.

It has variant readings: *bi-wariqikum* with a sukun on the *rāʾ*, which is the reading of Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and Khalaf; *waraqikum* with a sukun on the *rāʾ* and assimilation of the *qāf*, which is the reading of the people of Mecca; and *bi-wariqikum* with a fatha on the *wāw* and a kasra on the *rāʾ*, which is the reading of most reciters. *Warq* is like *kabid* and *kabid*, *kalimah* and *kalimah*.

"The city" is Ephesus. ﴿Let him see which of them has the purest food﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: the lawful slaughter, because most of them were Magians, though among them were believers who hid their faith. al-Dahhak said: the best. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: the finest. Yaman ibn Ruʾab said: the most cleanly. Qatadah said: the better. ʿIkrimah said: the more abundant.

The root of *zakāh* is increase and growth. The poet said:

*Our tribes are seven and you are three, / and the seven are purer and better than three.* [Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari 15/279.]

﴿Let him bring you provision from it﴾, that is, sustenance and food. ﴿And let him be gentle﴾: let him be gentle in buying, on his way, and in entering the city. ﴿And let him not make anyone aware of you﴾, that is, let him not inform anyone of you; that is, if he is discovered, he should not expose his companions to what would befall him.

﴿For if they come upon you﴾, that is, if they learn of your whereabouts, ﴿they will stone you﴾. Ibn Jurayj said: they will revile you and harm you with words. It is also said: they will kill you. It is also said: it was their custom to kill by stoning, which is among the most vile kinds of killing. It was also said: it is rebuke. ﴿Or they will return you to their religion﴾, which is unbelief. ﴿And you will never prosper, then, ever﴾ if you return to them.

﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾, that is, We made them known to people. It is said: "I came upon the thing" when I learned of it, and "I caused another to come upon it" when I informed him of it. ﴿That they might know that the promise of God is true﴾, meaning the people of Tidusius, ﴿and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾, ﴿when they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they disputed about the building and the mosque. The Muslims said: we will build a mosque over them, because they are upon our religion. The polytheists said: we will build a structure over them, because they are of our tradition. ʿIkrimah said: they disputed about spirits and bodies: the Muslims said the resurrection is of spirits and bodies, while some of them said the resurrection is of spirits without bodies; so God raised them from their sleep and showed them that resurrection is of spirits and bodies. It was also said: they disputed about the length of their stay. It was also said: they disputed about their number. ﴿They said: Build over them a structure; their Lord knows best about them﴾. ﴿Those who prevailed in their affair said: we will surely take over them a mosque﴾, meaning Tidusius the king and his companions. It was also said: those who prevailed over their affair were the believers. This returns to the first view.

﴿They will say: they were three﴾. This is because al-Sayyid and al-ʿAqib and their companions, Christians of Najran, were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and the mention of the People of the Cave came up. al-Sayyid said: "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog." al-Sayyid was a Jacobite. al-ʿAqib said: "They were five, the sixth of them being their dog." al-ʿAqib was a Nestorian. The Muslims said: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog." God confirmed the words of the Muslims and affirmed them after relating the words of the Christians, saying: ﴿They will say: they were three, the fourth of them their dog; and they will say: five, the sixth of them their dog, guessing at the unseen﴾ [Qur'an 18:22].

That is, throwing out a guess without certainty, like the saying of the poet:

*And I make the truth unseen, cast as a guess.* [Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari 15/282.]

﴿And they will say: seven, and the eighth of them their dog﴾. Some of them said: this *wāw* is the *wāw* of the eight; the Arabs say: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and eight, because their counting was in sevens, just as our counting today is in tens. A parallel is the words of God, exalted: ﴿The penitent, the worshippers, the praisers, the wanderers, the bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin right and forbid wrong, and those who keep the limits of God﴾ [Qur'an 9:112].

And His words describing the people of Paradise: ﴿Until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾ [Qur'an 39:73].

And His words to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Married women and virgins﴾ [Qur'an 66:5].

Some of them said: this is the *wāw* of judgement and verification. It is as if He relayed their disagreement, and the sentence was complete at His words ﴿and they will say: seven﴾, then He judged that the eighth of them was their dog, and the eighth can only come after the seven. This is the verification of the view of the Muslims. ﴿My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few﴾. Qatadah said: a few of mankind. ʿAṭa said: by "the few" are meant the People of the Book. Yahya ibn Abi Rawq narrated from his father, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning God's words ﴿none knows them except a few﴾, that he said: "I am among those few."

Their names were: Maksilmina, Tamlikha, Marṭunus, Sarinus, Anwanus, Rawanwanus, Mashtatiyunus, who was the shepherd; and the dog, whose name was Qiṭmīr, a reddish-black dog, above the *qaltī* (very short) and below the *kurdī* [see al-Qurtubi 10/384].

Muhammad ibn al-Musayyab said: *al-qaltī* is a Chinese dog. He said: "No narrator in Nishapur remained except that he wrote this hadith from me, except one for whom it was not destined." He said: "Abu ʿAmr and al-Hiyari wrote it from me."

﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾, that is, concerning their number and their affair, ﴿except with an outward argument﴾, which is what He related to him in His Book of their story. It means: what I have related to you is enough for you, so do not dispute about them. ﴿And do not seek a ruling about them from any of them﴾: from any of the People of the Book.

And ﴿you would see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right﴾. That is, *tazāwaru* (it inclines). The people of Kufa read it with the lighter form, dropping one of the two *zāʾ*s, while the people of Syria read *tazawwaru*, on the pattern of *taḥammaru*. All these readings have one meaning: it turns away from their cave to the right, meaning the right side. ﴿And when it sets, it passes them on the left﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it leaves them. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: it passes beyond them. The root meaning of *qarḍ* is cutting. ﴿While they were in a spacious part of it﴾, that is, an open space in the cave; its plural is *fajawāt* and *fajiyy*. God informed us of His preserving them in their resting place and made known His gentleness toward them in their lying down, and His choosing for them the best place for sleep. So He informed us that He had settled them in a sheltered part of the cave, facing the Bear (*banāt naʿsh*), so that the sun turned away from them whether rising, setting or passing, and did not enter upon them to harm them with its heat, change their colours or wear out their clothes. Yet they were in a spacious part where the cool breeze and its fragrance reached them, and it removed from them the distress and gloom of the cave. ﴿That is among the signs of God﴾: among the wonders of God's creation and the proofs of His power and wisdom. ﴿Whom God guides, he is the guided one; and whom He leads astray, you will not find for him any protecting friend to guide him﴾, because success and failure are in the hand of God, mighty and majestic.

﴿And you would think them awake, [O Muhammad]﴾, that is, alert, the plural of *yaqiẓ* and *yaqẓ*, like your saying *rajulun najdun* and *najdun* for a brave man, whose plural is *anjād*. ﴿While they were asleep﴾: *ruqūd*, sleeping, the plural of *rāqid*, like *qāʿid* and *quʿūd*. ﴿And We turned them over﴾; al-Hasan read *wa-nuqlibuhum* with the lighter form, ﴿to the right and to the left﴾, once onto the right side and once onto the left side. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they would turn over once each year from one side to the other, lest the earth consume their flesh. It is said that the Day of ʿAshura was the day of their turning. Abu Hurayrah said: they had two turnings every year. ﴿And their dog﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said it was reddish-black (*anmar*). Muqatil said it was yellow. al-Qurazi said its yellowness tended toward redness. al-Kalbi said its colour was like *khalanj* (a tree, arabicised; note from the manuscript). It was also said: the colour of the stone; and it was said: the colour of the sky.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) said: "Its name was Rayyan."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: Qiṭmīr. al-Awzaʿi said: Nataw. Shuʿayb al-Jubbaʾi said: Ḥumrān. ʿAbdullah ibn Kathir: the dog's name was Qiṭmūr. [Qala] (not in the approved copy). al-Suddi: Nūn. ʿAbdullah ibn Salam: Basīṭ. Kaʿb: Aṣhab. Wahb: Naqiyy; it was also said: Qiṭfīr.

From ʿUmar, who said: "Among the things taken as a covenant from the scorpion is that it should not harm anyone by night or by day: ﴿Peace upon Noah﴾. Their names were: Maksilmina, Tamlikha, Marṭunus, Sarinus, Anwanus, Rawanwanus, Mashtatiyunus, who was the shepherd; and the dog, whose name was Qiṭmīr, a reddish-black dog, above the *qaltī* (very short) and below the *kurdī* [see al-Qurtubi 10/384].

Muhammad ibn al-Musayyab said: *al-qaltī* is a Chinese dog. He said: "No narrator in Nishapur remained except that he wrote this hadith from me, except one for whom it was not destined." He said: "Abu ʿAmr and al-Hiyari wrote it from me."

﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾, that is, concerning their number and their affair, ﴿except with an outward argument﴾, which is what He related to him in His Book of their story. It means: what I have related to you is enough for you, so do not dispute about them. ﴿And do not seek a ruling about them from any of them﴾: from any of the People of the Book.

And ﴿you would see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right﴾. That is, *tazāwaru* (it inclines). The people of Kufa read it with the lighter form, dropping one of the two *zāʾ*s, while the people of Syria read *tazawwaru*, on the pattern of *taḥammaru*. All these readings have one meaning: it turns away from their cave to the right, meaning the right side. ﴿And when it sets, it passes them on the left﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it leaves them. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: it passes beyond them. The root meaning of *qarḍ* is cutting. ﴿While they were in a spacious part of it﴾, that is, an open space in the cave; its plural is *fajawāt* and *fajiyy*. God informed us of His preserving them in their resting place and made known His gentleness toward them in their lying down, and His choosing for them the best place for sleep. So He informed us that He had settled them in a sheltered part of the cave, facing the Bear (*banāt naʿsh*), so that the sun turned away from them whether rising, setting or passing, and did not enter upon them to harm them with its heat, change their colours or wear out their clothes. Yet they were in a spacious part where the cool breeze and its fragrance reached them, and it removed from them the distress and gloom of the cave. ﴿That is among the signs of God﴾: among the wonders of God's creation and the proofs of His power and wisdom. ﴿Whom God guides, he is the guided one; and whom He leads astray, you will not find for him any protecting friend to guide him﴾, because success and failure are in the hand of God, mighty and majestic.

﴿And you would think them awake, [O Muhammad]﴾, that is, alert, the plural of *yaqiẓ* and *yaqẓ*, like your saying *rajulun najdun* and *najdun* for a brave man, whose plural is *anjād*. ﴿While they were asleep﴾: *ruqūd*, sleeping, the plural of *rāqid*, like *qāʿid* and *quʿūd*. ﴿And We turned them over﴾; al-Hasan read *wa-nuqlibuhum* with the lighter form, ﴿to the right and to the left﴾, once onto the right side and once onto the left side. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they would turn over once each year from one side to the other, lest the earth consume their flesh. It is said that the Day of ʿAshura was the day of their turning. Abu Hurayrah said: they had two turnings every year. ﴿And their dog﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said it was reddish-black (*anmar*). Muqatil said it was yellow. al-Qurazi said its yellowness tended toward redness. al-Kalbi said its colour was like *khalanj* (a tree, arabicised; note from the manuscript). It was also said: the colour of the stone; and it was said: the colour of the sky.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) said: "Its name was Rayyan."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: Qiṭmīr. al-Awzaʿi said: Nataw. Shuʿayb al-Jubbaʾi said: Ḥumrān. ʿAbdullah ibn Kathir: the dog's name was Qiṭmūr. [Qala] (not in the approved copy). al-Suddi: Nūn. ʿAbdullah ibn Salam: Basīṭ. Kaʿb: Aṣhab. Wahb: Naqiyy; it was also said: Qiṭfīr.

From ʿUmar, who said: "Among the things taken as a covenant from the scorpion is that it should not harm anyone by night or by day: ﴿Peace upon Noah﴾. And among the things taken as a covenant from the dog is that it should not harm whoever mounts it, by saying: ﴿And their dog, stretching out his forelegs at the threshold﴾."

Jaʿfar al-Sadiq read *wa-Kalibuhum*, meaning the owner of the dog.

﴿Stretching out his forelegs at the threshold﴾. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: *al-waṣīd* is the courtyard of the cave; this is also the narration of ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: *al-waṣīd* is *al-ṣaʿīd*, which is dust; this is the narration of ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas. al-Suddi said: *al-waṣīd* is the door; this is the narration of ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and he recited:

*In an open land whose gate is not closed, / upon me, and my known (goodness) there is no denial.* [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 10/373; Zad al-Masir 5/83.]

That is, its door. ʿAṭa said: *al-waṣīd* is the threshold of the door. al-Qutabi said: *al-waṣīd* is the building; its root is from the Arabs' saying *aṣadtu al-bāb* and *awṣadtuhu*, meaning I closed it and shut it tight.

﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight﴾, because God had clothed them with such an appearance that no one could reach them and no hand could touch them until the Book reached its term, and then God would awaken them from their sleep, by the will of God, mighty and majestic, to make them a sign and a lesson for whomever of His creatures He wills. ﴿That they might know that the promise of God is true, and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾ [Qur'an 18:21].

﴿And you would have been filled with terror from them﴾: fear. The people of Medina read *lamulli'ta* with doubling. It was also said: this was only from the loneliness of the place they were in. al-Kalbi said: because their eyes were open, like one awake who wants to speak, while they were asleep. It was also said: God restrained them with terror so that no one would see them. Saʿid ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "We fought with Muʿawiyah the battle of al-Mudayiq toward the Romans, and we passed by the cave in which were the People of the Cave. Muʿawiyah said: 'If only it were revealed to us about these people, so that we could look at them!' Ibn ʿAbbas said: 'That is not for you; God has restrained someone better than you.' He said: ﴿If you had looked upon them you would have turned away from them in flight, and you would have been filled with terror from them﴾." Then Muʿawiyah said: "I will not stop until I know their state." So he sent some men and said: "Go and look." They did so, but when they entered the cave God sent a wind upon them that drove them out, and they could not look at them because of the terror.

﴿And thus We raised them up﴾: that is, just as We put them to sleep in the cave and prevented anyone from reaching them, and preserved their bodies from decay over the length of time, and their clothes from mould over the passing of days, by Our power. ﴿Thus We raised them up﴾ from that sleep which resembles death, ﴿that they might question one another﴾: that they might speak and ask one another. ﴿A speaker among them said﴾: that is, their leader, Maksilmina: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ For they were startled at their own long sleep. It is also said: what troubled them was the prayers they had missed, so they said that. ﴿They said: We have remained a day﴾, for they had entered the cave in the early morning; when they saw the sun they said ﴿or part of a day﴾, guarding against lying, since some of the sun's light still remained. It is also said: it was after the sun had passed its zenith. When they looked at their hair and nails, they were certain that their stay was more than a day or part of a day, and so ﴿they said: Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾. It is also said: when their leader heard the disagreement among them, he said that.

﴿So send one of you﴾, that is, Tamlikha, ﴿with this silver of yours to the city﴾. *Al-wariq* is silver, whether minted or unminted. The evidence for this is that ʿUrfajah ibn Asʿad had his nose struck off on the day of al-Kilab, so he made a nose of silver, which then stank upon him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to make a nose of gold.

It has variant readings: *bi-wariqikum* with a sukun on the *rāʾ*, which is the reading of Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and Khalaf; *waraqikum* with a sukun on the *rāʾ* and assimilation of the *qāf*, which is the reading of the people of Mecca; and *bi-wariqikum* with a fatha on the *wāw* and a kasra on the *rāʾ*, which is the reading of most reciters. *Warq* is like *kabid* and *kabid*, *kalimah* and *kalimah*.

"The city" is Ephesus. ﴿Let him see which of them has the purest food﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: the lawful slaughter, because most of them were Magians, though among them were believers who hid their faith. al-Dahhak said: the best. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: the finest. Yaman ibn Ruʾab said: the most cleanly. Qatadah said: the better. ʿIkrimah said: the more abundant.

The root of *zakāh* is increase and growth. The poet said:

*Our tribes are seven and you are three, / and the seven are purer and better than three.* [Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari 15/279.]

﴿Let him bring you provision from it﴾, that is, sustenance and food. ﴿And let him be gentle﴾: let him be gentle in buying, on his way, and in entering the city. ﴿And let him not make anyone aware of you﴾, that is, let him not inform anyone of you; that is, if he is discovered, he should not expose his companions to what would befall him.

﴿For if they come upon you﴾, that is, if they learn of your whereabouts, ﴿they will stone you﴾. Ibn Jurayj said: they will revile you and harm you with words. It is also said: they will kill you. It is also said: it was their custom to kill by stoning, which is among the most vile kinds of killing. It was also said: it is rebuke. ﴿Or they will return you to their religion﴾, which is unbelief. ﴿And you will never prosper, then, ever﴾ if you return to them.

﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾, that is, We made them known to people. It is said: "I came upon the thing" when I learned of it, and "I caused another to come upon it" when I informed him of it. ﴿That they might know that the promise of God is true﴾, meaning the people of Tidusius, ﴿and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾, ﴿when they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they disputed about the building and the mosque. The Muslims said: we will build a mosque over them, because they are upon our religion. The polytheists said: we will build a structure over them, because they are of our tradition. ʿIkrimah said: they disputed about spirits and bodies: the Muslims said the resurrection is of spirits and bodies, while some of them said the resurrection is of spirits without bodies; so God raised them from their sleep and showed them that resurrection is of spirits and bodies. It was also said: they disputed about the length of their stay. It was also said: they disputed about their number. ﴿They said: Build over them a structure; their Lord knows best about them﴾. ﴿Those who prevailed in their affair said: we will surely take over them a mosque﴾, meaning Tidusius the king and his companions. It was also said: those who prevailed over their affair were the believers. This returns to the first view.

﴿They will say: they were three﴾. This is because al-Sayyid and al-ʿAqib and their companions, Christians of Najran, were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and the mention of the People of the Cave came up. al-Sayyid said: "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog." al-Sayyid was a Jacobite. al-ʿAqib said: "They were five, the sixth of them being their dog." al-ʿAqib was a Nestorian. The Muslims said: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog." God confirmed the words of the Muslims and affirmed them after relating the words of the Christians, saying: ﴿They will say: they were three, the fourth of them their dog; and they will say: five, the sixth of them their dog, guessing at the unseen﴾ [Qur'an 18:22].

That is, throwing out a guess without certainty, like the saying of the poet:

*And I make the truth unseen, cast as a guess.* [Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari 15/282.]

﴿And they will say: seven, and the eighth of them their dog﴾. Some of them said: this *wāw* is the *wāw* of the eight; the Arabs say: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and eight, because their counting was in sevens, just as our counting today is in tens. A parallel is the words of God, exalted: ﴿The penitent, the worshippers, the praisers, the wanderers, the bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin right and forbid wrong, and those who keep the limits of God﴾ [Qur'an 9:112].

And His words describing the people of Paradise: ﴿Until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾ [Qur'an 39:73].

And His words to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Married women and virgins﴾ [Qur'an 66:5].

Some of them said: this is the *wāw* of judgement and verification. It is as if He relayed their disagreement, and the sentence was complete at His words ﴿and they will say: seven﴾, then He judged that the eighth of them was their dog, and the eighth can only come after the seven. This is the verification of the view of the Muslims. ﴿My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few﴾. Qatadah said: a few of mankind. ʿAṭa said: by "the few" are meant the People of the Book. Yahya ibn Abi Rawq narrated from his father, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning God's words ﴿none knows them except a few﴾, that he said: "I am among those few."

Their names were: Maksilmina, Tamlikha, Marṭunus, Sarinus, Anwanus, Rawanwanus, Mashtatiyunus, who was the shepherd; and the dog, whose name was Qiṭmīr, a reddish-black dog, above the *qaltī* (very short) and below the *kurdī* [see al-Qurtubi 10/384].

Muhammad ibn al-Musayyab said: *al-qaltī* is a Chinese dog. He said: "No narrator in Nishapur remained except that he wrote this hadith from me, except one for whom it was not destined." He said: "Abu ʿAmr and al-Hiyari wrote it from me."

﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾, that is, concerning their number and their affair, ﴿except with an outward argument﴾, which is what He related to him in His Book of their story. It means: what I have related to you is enough for you, so do not dispute about them. ﴿And do not seek a ruling about them from any of them﴾: from any of the People of the Book.

And say not of anything, "I will surely do that tomorrow," without adding, "if God wills." ﴿And say not of anything, "I will surely do that tomorrow," unless God wills.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: this means that when you resolve to do something tomorrow, or swear an oath about something, you should say, "I will do that tomorrow, if God wills." And if you forget the exception and then remember it, say it even after a year. This is a discipline from God to His Prophet (ﷺ), when he was asked about three matters: the People of the Cave, the Spirit, and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he promised to inform them without adding the exception.

'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id al-Maqri narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A servant's faith is not complete until he makes the exception [[i.e., until he says, "If God wills"]] in every statement he makes." [68]

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Hasan said: its meaning is: when you forget the exception and then remember, make the exception. 'Ikrimah said: its meaning is: remember your Lord when you become angry.

'Abd al-Samad ibn Hassan narrated to us, from Wuhayb, who said: It is written in the Gospel: "Son of Adam, remember Me when you are angry, and I will remember you when I am angry, and I will not destroy you among those who are destroyed. And when you are wronged, do not seek vengeance, for My support for you is better than your support for yourself." Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: this refers to the prayer, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever forgets a prayer or sleeps through it, let him pray it when he remembers it." [[Sunan al-Darimi: 1/280.]] [69]

The people of allusion (ahl al-isharah, Sufi interpreters) said: its meaning is ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ other than Him, because the remembrance of God Most High is realized only after forgetting other things. This is supported by the saying of Dhu al-Nun al-Misri: "Whoever remembers God with true remembrance forgets everything in comparison with His remembrance; and when he forgets everything in comparison with His remembrance, God preserves everything for him, and it becomes his substitute for everything." It was also said: its meaning is: remember your Lord when you abandon His remembrance, and forgetting is abandoning.

﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this."﴾ That is, He will keep me on a path nearer to Him, so I will be guided. It was also said: the meaning is, perhaps God will guide and direct me to something nearer than what I promised you and told you would happen, if He wills. It was also said: God commanded him to remember Him whenever he forgets something, and to ask Him to make him remember, so that he recalls, or to guide him to what is better for him than recalling what he forgot.

It is said that when the people asked him about the story of the People of the Cave, out of obstinacy, God commanded him to inform them that God would give him proofs and clear evidence of the truth of his prophethood and of the truth to which he called them, and would guide them to what they asked. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, did so, when He gave him knowledge of the unseen matters of the messengers and their news, which was clearer as proof and closer to right guidance than the story of the People of the Cave. Some of them said: this is something he was commanded to say along with ﴿unless God wills﴾ when he remembers the exception after forgetting it. So when a person forgets, God gives him [[so in the manuscript facsimile]] from that. Its expiation is to say: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this.﴾

﴿And they remained﴾, that is, the People of the Cave, ﴿in their cave﴾. Some said: this is a report about the People of the Scripture, that they said this, and they said: if it were a report from God, Mighty and Majestic, about the exact duration of their stay in the cave, then His saying ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾ would have no understandable sense, and He had already informed His creatures of the length of their stay. This is the view of Qatadah.

It is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And they said: they remained in their cave." Mutar al-Warraq said regarding this verse: this is something the Jews said, and God refuted them, saying: ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained.﴾ Others said: this is God's report about the exact duration of their stay in the cave. They said: the meaning of His saying ﴿Say: God knows best﴾ is that the People of the Scripture said in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "For the youths, from the time they entered the cave until today, is three hundred and nine years." God, Mighty and Majestic, refuted that, saying: ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾ after He took their souls, until today. None knows that except God and whomever God has informed of it. Al-Kalbi said: the Christians of Najran said: "As for the three hundred, we know it, but as for the nine, we have no knowledge of them," so it was revealed: ﴿God knows best how long they remained.﴾

"Three hundred years" in the genitive construction without tanwin, was recited by Hamzah and al-Kisa'i; the others recite it with tanwin, meaning: and they remained in their cave three hundred years. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: the revelation came ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred [years]﴾ and they said: "Days or years?" So it was revealed, "years" (sinin), and therefore He said "years" and did not say "year." ﴿And they added nine.﴾ ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained. His is the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears!﴾ That means: how much God sees everything that exists! And how much He hears everything that is heard! ﴿They have no protector besides Him﴾, that is, the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth have no protector apart from God, ﴿no helper﴾: a supporter. ﴿And He does not share His command with anyone﴾, [meaning] among the idols or others.

﴿And recite﴾, that is, read, O Muhammad, ﴿what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾, meaning: the Qur'an, and follow what is in it. ﴿None can alter His words﴾. Al-Kalbi said: none can change the Qur'an. Muhammad ibn Jarir said: that is, none can change what He has threatened with His words against the people of disobedience and those who oppose His Book. ﴿And you will never find, other than Him, a refuge﴾, if you do not follow the Qur'an and oppose it. Ibn 'Abbas said: a shelter. al-Hasan said: a place of entry. It was said: a place of deviation. It was said: a refuge. Mujahid said: a shelter; its root is from inclining, and from it comes the word "lahd" (the niche of a grave).

﴿And restrain yourself﴾ – the verse –

The exegetes said: it was revealed concerning 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari, because he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) before this verse was revealed, and with him were Bilal, Suhayb, Khabbab, 'Ammar, 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Mihja' and Salman. Salman was wearing a cloak in which he had been sweating, and in his hand was a palm frond which he was splitting and weaving. 'Uyaynah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Does the smell of these people not bother you? By God, their smell has harmed us." He said: "We are the masters and nobles of Mudar. If we embrace Islam, the people will embrace Islam; and if we refuse, the people will refuse. Nothing prevents us from following you except these people. So remove them, until we follow you, and make for us a gathering and for them a gathering."

Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And restrain yourself﴾, that is, hold yourself ﴿with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾: who worship their Lord and honor Him, ﴿seeking His face﴾, that is, seeking God, Mighty and Majestic, not seeking any worldly gain. What is meant is good deeds and abandoning showing off. Qatadah said: that means the dawn and afternoon prayers. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: By Him in whose hand my soul is, they are the people of the obligatory prayers. Qatadah said: this verse was revealed concerning the People of the Suffah, who were seven hundred poor men who kept to the mosque of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), not returning to trade, nor to crops, nor to livestock; they would pray one prayer and wait for another.

Qatadah said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "Praise be to God who has placed in my community those with whom I was commanded to be patient." [[Musnad Abi Ya'la: 2/383.]] [70]

﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾: do not turn your eyes away from them toward others, ﴿desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾, meaning sitting with the leaders, the rich, and the nobles.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾, desiring worldly adornment, while they are immersed in seeking forgiveness, because that would be a judgment against the Prophet (ﷺ) for desiring this world. ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾, that is, whose heart We left and made forget Our remembrance. Abu al-'Aliyah said: this means Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. Others said: it means 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn. ﴿And he followed his desire, and his affair was [ever] neglect﴾. Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: lost. Dawud said: regret. Habbab said: destruction. Ibn Zayd said: opposing the truth. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: excess. al-Akhfash said: exceeding the limit. al-Farra' said: abandoned. It was said: vain. Abu Zayd al-Balkhi said: going ahead in evil. Abu 'Ubayd said: it comes from the saying of the Arabs: "a horse, a fars-fart," when it outruns the other horses; and "the word of mine was farat," meaning it preceded. It was also said: its meaning is that he wasted his affair and left his days idle. They said: the believer is one who uses his time, and time does not use him.

﴿And say: the truth is from your Lord﴾. "The truth" is nominative as a quotation (hikayah). It was also said it is nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "And say: it is the truth from your Lord," that is, what was mentioned of the Qur'an, faith, and the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said it is nominative as the subject, with its predicate being "from your Lord." The meaning of the verse: Say, O Muhammad, to those whose hearts We made heedless of Our remembrance: O people, the truth is from your Lord, and to Him belongs success and abandonment, and in His hand is misguidance and guidance; He guides whom He wills to believe, and misguides whom He wills to disbelieve. [[In the Isfahan copy: "then let him disbelieve." (Marginal note of the Isfahan copy.)]] Nothing of that is up to me. I am not driving away the believers for your sake. If you wish, believe; and if you wish, disbelieve. For if you disbelieve, your Lord has prepared for your disbelief a fire whose enclosure surrounds you; and if you believe and obey, then for you is what God, Mighty and Majestic, has described for the people of His obedience.

His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ is not a permission or choice; rather it is a warning and threat, like His saying: ﴿Do what you will.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever God wills faith for, believes, and whoever God wills disbelief for, disbelieves. This is His saying: ﴿And you do not will, except that God wills.﴾

﴿Indeed, We have prepared﴾: We prepared and made ready, from "al-'utad," which is equipment. ﴿For the wrongdoers﴾: for the disbelievers, ﴿a Fire﴾. In it is evidence that the Fire is created, for if it were not created and existing and prepared, the one who informed would be a liar, and God is exalted above that.

His saying: ﴿Its enclosure surrounds them﴾.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The enclosure of the Fire is four walls, thick, each one a distance of forty years." [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 15/298.]] [71]

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a wall of fire.

Al-Kalbi said: it is a neck that comes out of the Fire and encircles the disbelievers like an enclosure. Al-Qutaybi said: the "saradiq" is the chamber that surrounds the tent. Ru'bah said:

"O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud... the enclosure of glory is extended over you."

Salamah ibn Jandal said:

"He is the one who admitted al-Nu'man into a house whose roof is... the chests of elephants, after a tent that is enclosed."

Here it means the smoke that will surround the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, which God mentioned in Surat al-Mursalat: ﴿Proceed to a shadow of three branches.﴾ [[Surat al-Mursalat: 30.]]

﴿And if they seek relief﴾ from the intensity of thirst, ﴿they will be given relief with water like molten brass﴾.

Abu Muslim narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding ﴿water like molten brass﴾, he said: "Like the dregs of oil; when it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off into it." [[Musnad Ahmad: 3/71.]] [72] Ibn 'Abbas said: thick water like the sediment of oil. al-A'mash said: it is the residue of oil. Mujahid said: pus and blood. al-Dahhak said: al-muhl is black water, and Hell is black, its water is black, its trees are black, and its people are black. Abu 'Ubaydah said: everything that is melted from the substances of the earth.

Rawh ibn 'Ubadah narrated from Sa'id, from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that a vessel of gold and silver was presented to Ibn Mas'ud. He ordered a trench to be dug in the ground, then fuel of good firewood was thrown in, then that vessel was thrown into it. When it foamed and melted, he said to his servant: "Call whoever is present from the people of Kufa." He called a group, and when they entered upon him, he said: "Do you see this?" They said: "Yes." He said: "We have never seen in this world anything more similar to al-muhl than this gold and silver when it foamed and melted." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: al-muhl is that whose heat has reached its extreme.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: I heard al-Muntaji' ibn Nabhan mention a man, and he said: "He is more hateful to me than al-tulya and al-muhl." I said to him: "What is al-muhl?" He said: "It is a crust that is cut from the sides of the bread by fire, bright red, very red, as if it were a pomegranate; it is a live coal." Al-tulya: the she-camel smeared with tar. ﴿It scorches the faces.﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: When the people of the Fire become hungry, they seek relief from the tree of Zaqqum, and they eat from it, and their skins and faces are peeled off, so that if a passerby came who knew them, he would recognize their faces by the skins of their faces in it. Then thirst overtakes them, and they seek relief, and they are given relief with ﴿water like molten brass﴾, which is that whose heat has reached its extreme. When they bring it near their mouths, the flesh of their faces, from which the skin has fallen, is roasted by its heat. ﴿Wretched is the drink, and evil is the Fire as a resting place﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: a dwelling. Mujahid: a gathering place. 'Ata': a place of rest. It was said: a cushion. al-Qutaybi said: a seat. The root of "murtafaq" is a reclining place; it is said of it: "irtafaqtu" when I leaned on a reclining place. The poet said:

"She said to him, and he leaned, 'Ah, is there a youth who drives the people with the gazelles of the forenoon?'" [[Jami' al-Bayan: 15/300.]]

It is also said: "irtafaqa al-rajul," when a man spends the night on his elbow, unable to sleep. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

"The one free of care slept, and I spent the night leaning on my elbow, as if in my eyes is bitter aloe that has been slaughtered." [[Jami' al-Bayan: 15/301; Lisan al-'Arab: 4/397, where it reads "mushtajiran" instead of "murtafiqan."]]

That is, cut off from its support. The "sabb" is a tree which, when uprooted, exudes something like milk, and sometimes a speck rises from it, which falls into the eye, so that it is like a spark of fire, and sometimes weakens the sight. It may also be that His saying "murtafaqan" comes from "rifq," meaning kindness and benefit.

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good work.﴾ His saying "Indeed, We do not waste" is not the predicate of "Indeed, those who believe," but rather a parenthetical statement, and the predicate of the first "inna" (the one at the beginning of the verse) is His saying: ﴿those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾. Similar to this in speech is common; the poet said:

"Indeed the Caliph—indeed God has clothed him with the garment of kingship, by which the endings are hoped for."

Some said: there is an omission in it, for its meaning is: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—then indeed We do not waste their reward but reward them.﴾

Then He mentioned the reward, saying: ﴿those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾, which is an abiding dwelling. ﴿Beneath them rivers will flow﴾. ﴿They will be adorned﴾: they will wear therein ﴿bracelets﴾, which is the plural of "aswar." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: each one of them will be adorned with three bracelets: one of silver, one of gold, and one of pearls and rubies. ﴿of gold﴾. ﴿And they will wear green garments of fine silk﴾, which is what is thin of brocade, ﴿and brocade﴾, which is what is thick of it. It was said: it is a Persian word that has been Arabized. ﴿Reclining therein﴾: in the gardens ﴿on couches﴾, which are thrones in canopies, the singular of which is "arikah." ﴿How excellent the reward, and how good the resting place﴾ — meaning the gardens.

And say not of anything, "I will surely do that tomorrow," without adding, "if God wills." ﴿And say not of anything, "I will surely do that tomorrow," unless God wills.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: this means that when you resolve to do something tomorrow, or swear an oath about something, you should say, "I will do that tomorrow, if God wills." And if you forget the exception and then remember it, say it even after a year. This is a discipline from God to His Prophet (ﷺ), when he was asked about three matters: the People of the Cave, the Spirit, and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he promised to inform them without adding the exception.

'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id al-Maqri narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A servant's faith is not complete until he makes the exception [[i.e., until he says, "If God wills"]] in every statement he makes." [68]

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Hasan said: its meaning is: when you forget the exception and then remember, make the exception. 'Ikrimah said: its meaning is: remember your Lord when you become angry.

'Abd al-Samad ibn Hassan narrated to us, from Wuhayb, who said: It is written in the Gospel: "Son of Adam, remember Me when you are angry, and I will remember you when I am angry, and I will not destroy you among those who are destroyed. And when you are wronged, do not seek vengeance, for My support for you is better than your support for yourself." Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: this refers to the prayer, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever forgets a prayer or sleeps through it, let him pray it when he remembers it." [[Sunan al-Darimi: 1/280.]] [69]

The people of allusion (ahl al-isharah, Sufi interpreters) said: its meaning is ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ other than Him, because the remembrance of God Most High is realized only after forgetting other things. This is supported by the saying of Dhu al-Nun al-Misri: "Whoever remembers God with true remembrance forgets everything in comparison with His remembrance; and when he forgets everything in comparison with His remembrance, God preserves everything for him, and it becomes his substitute for everything." It was also said: its meaning is: remember your Lord when you abandon His remembrance, and forgetting is abandoning.

﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this."﴾ That is, He will keep me on a path nearer to Him, so I will be guided. It was also said: the meaning is, perhaps God will guide and direct me to something nearer than what I promised you and told you would happen, if He wills. It was also said: God commanded him to remember Him whenever he forgets something, and to ask Him to make him remember, so that he recalls, or to guide him to what is better for him than recalling what he forgot.

It is said that when the people asked him about the story of the People of the Cave, out of obstinacy, God commanded him to inform them that God would give him proofs and clear evidence of the truth of his prophethood and of the truth to which he called them, and would guide them to what they asked. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, did so, when He gave him knowledge of the unseen matters of the messengers and their news, which was clearer as proof and closer to right guidance than the story of the People of the Cave. Some of them said: this is something he was commanded to say along with ﴿unless God wills﴾ when he remembers the exception after forgetting it. So when a person forgets, God gives him [[so in the manuscript facsimile]] from that. Its expiation is to say: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this.﴾

﴿And they remained﴾, that is, the People of the Cave, ﴿in their cave﴾. Some said: this is a report about the People of the Scripture, that they said this, and they said: if it were a report from God, Mighty and Majestic, about the exact duration of their stay in the cave, then His saying ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾ would have no understandable sense, and He had already informed His creatures of the length of their stay. This is the view of Qatadah.

It is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And they said: they remained in their cave." Mutar al-Warraq said regarding this verse: this is something the Jews said, and God refuted them, saying: ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained.﴾ Others said: this is God's report about the exact duration of their stay in the cave. They said: the meaning of His saying ﴿Say: God knows best﴾ is that the People of the Scripture said in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "For the youths, from the time they entered the cave until today, is three hundred and nine years." God, Mighty and Majestic, refuted that, saying: ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾ after He took their souls, until today. None knows that except God and whomever God has informed of it. Al-Kalbi said: the Christians of Najran said: "As for the three hundred, we know it, but as for the nine, we have no knowledge of them," so it was revealed: ﴿God knows best how long they remained.﴾

"Three hundred years" in the genitive construction without tanwin, was recited by Hamzah and al-Kisa'i; the others recite it with tanwin, meaning: and they remained in their cave three hundred years. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: the revelation came ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred [years]﴾ and they said: "Days or years?" So it was revealed, "years" (sinin), and therefore He said "years" and did not say "year." ﴿And they added nine.﴾ ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained. His is the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears!﴾ That means: how much God sees everything that exists! And how much He hears everything that is heard! ﴿They have no protector besides Him﴾, that is, the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth have no protector apart from God, ﴿no helper﴾: a supporter. ﴿And He does not share His command with anyone﴾, [meaning] among the idols or others.

﴿And recite﴾, that is, read, O Muhammad, ﴿what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾, meaning: the Qur'an, and follow what is in it. ﴿None can alter His words﴾. Al-Kalbi said: none can change the Qur'an. Muhammad ibn Jarir said: that is, none can change what He has threatened with His words against the people of disobedience and those who oppose His Book. ﴿And you will never find, other than Him, a refuge﴾, if you do not follow the Qur'an and oppose it. Ibn 'Abbas said: a shelter. al-Hasan said: a place of entry. It was said: a place of deviation. It was said: a refuge. Mujahid said: a shelter; its root is from inclining, and from it comes the word "lahd" (the niche of a grave).

﴿And restrain yourself﴾ – the verse –

The exegetes said: it was revealed concerning 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari, because he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) before this verse was revealed, and with him were Bilal, Suhayb, Khabbab, 'Ammar, 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Mihja' and Salman. Salman was wearing a cloak in which he had been sweating, and in his hand was a palm frond which he was splitting and weaving. 'Uyaynah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Does the smell of these people not bother you? By God, their smell has harmed us." He said: "We are the masters and nobles of Mudar. If we embrace Islam, the people will embrace Islam; and if we refuse, the people will refuse. Nothing prevents us from following you except these people. So remove them, until we follow you, and make for us a gathering and for them a gathering."

Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And restrain yourself﴾, that is, hold yourself ﴿with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾: who worship their Lord and honor Him, ﴿seeking His face﴾, that is, seeking God, Mighty and Majestic, not seeking any worldly gain. What is meant is good deeds and abandoning showing off. Qatadah said: that means the dawn and afternoon prayers. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: By Him in whose hand my soul is, they are the people of the obligatory prayers. Qatadah said: this verse was revealed concerning the People of the Suffah, who were seven hundred poor men who kept to the mosque of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), not returning to trade, nor to crops, nor to livestock; they would pray one prayer and wait for another.

Qatadah said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "Praise be to God who has placed in my community those with whom I was commanded to be patient." [[Musnad Abi Ya'la: 2/383.]] [70]

﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾: do not turn your eyes away from them toward others, ﴿desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾, meaning sitting with the leaders, the rich, and the nobles.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾, desiring worldly adornment, while they are immersed in seeking forgiveness, because that would be a judgment against the Prophet (ﷺ) for desiring this world. ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾, that is, whose heart We left and made forget Our remembrance. Abu al-'Aliyah said: this means Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. Others said: it means 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn. ﴿And he followed his desire, and his affair was [ever] neglect﴾. Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: lost. Dawud said: regret. Habbab said: destruction. Ibn Zayd said: opposing the truth. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: excess. al-Akhfash said: exceeding the limit. al-Farra' said: abandoned. It was said: vain. Abu Zayd al-Balkhi said: going ahead in evil. Abu 'Ubayd said: it comes from the saying of the Arabs: "a horse, a fars-fart," when it outruns the other horses; and "the word of mine was farat," meaning it preceded. It was also said: its meaning is that he wasted his affair and left his days idle. They said: the believer is one who uses his time, and time does not use him.

﴿And say: the truth is from your Lord﴾. "The truth" is nominative as a quotation (hikayah). It was also said it is nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "And say: it is the truth from your Lord," that is, what was mentioned of the Qur'an, faith, and the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said it is nominative as the subject, with its predicate being "from your Lord." The meaning of the verse: Say, O Muhammad, to those whose hearts We made heedless of Our remembrance: O people, the truth is from your Lord, and to Him belongs success and abandonment, and in His hand is misguidance and guidance; He guides whom He wills to believe, and misguides whom He wills to disbelieve. [[In the Isfahan copy: "then let him disbelieve." (Marginal note of the Isfahan copy.)]] Nothing of that is up to me. I am not driving away the believers for your sake. If you wish, believe; and if you wish, disbelieve. For if you disbelieve, your Lord has prepared for your disbelief a fire whose enclosure surrounds you; and if you believe and obey, then for you is what God, Mighty and Majestic, has described for the people of His obedience.

His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ is not a permission or choice; rather it is a warning and threat, like His saying: ﴿Do what you will.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever God wills faith for, believes, and whoever God wills disbelief for, disbelieves. This is His saying: ﴿And you do not will, except that God wills.﴾

﴿Indeed, We have prepared﴾: We prepared and made ready, from "al-'utad," which is equipment. ﴿For the wrongdoers﴾: for the disbelievers, ﴿a Fire﴾. In it is evidence that the Fire is created, for if it were not created and existing and prepared, the one who informed would be a liar, and God is exalted above that.

His saying: ﴿Its enclosure surrounds them﴾.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The enclosure of the Fire is four walls, thick, each one a distance of forty years." [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 15/298.]] [71]

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a wall of fire.

Al-Kalbi said: it is a neck that comes out of the Fire and encircles the disbelievers like an enclosure. Al-Qutaybi said: the "saradiq" is the chamber that surrounds the tent. Ru'bah said:

"O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud... the enclosure of glory is extended over you."

Salamah ibn Jandal said:

"He is the one who admitted al-Nu'man into a house whose roof is... the chests of elephants, after a tent that is enclosed."

Here it means the smoke that will surround the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, which God mentioned in Surat al-Mursalat: ﴿Proceed to a shadow of three branches.﴾ [[Surat al-Mursalat: 30.]]

﴿And if they seek relief﴾ from the intensity of thirst, ﴿they will be given relief with water like molten brass﴾.

Abu Muslim narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding ﴿water like molten brass﴾, he said: "Like the dregs of oil; when it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off into it." [[Musnad Ahmad: 3/71.]] [72] Ibn 'Abbas said: thick water like the sediment of oil. al-A'mash said: it is the residue of oil. Mujahid said: pus and blood. al-Dahhak said: al-muhl is black water, and Hell is black, its water is black, its trees are black, and its people are black. Abu 'Ubaydah said: everything that is melted from the substances of the earth.

Rawh ibn 'Ubadah narrated from Sa'id, from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that a vessel of gold and silver was presented to Ibn Mas'ud. He ordered a trench to be dug in the ground, then fuel of good firewood was thrown in, then that vessel was thrown into it. When it foamed and melted, he said to his servant: "Call whoever is present from the people of Kufa." He called a group, and when they entered upon him, he said: "Do you see this?" They said: "Yes." He said: "We have never seen in this world anything more similar to al-muhl than this gold and silver when it foamed and melted." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: al-muhl is that whose heat has reached its extreme.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: I heard al-Muntaji' ibn Nabhan mention a man, and he said: "He is more hateful to me than al-tulya and al-muhl." I said to him: "What is al-muhl?" He said: "It is a crust that is cut from the sides of the bread by fire, bright red, very red, as if it were a pomegranate; it is a live coal." Al-tulya: the she-camel smeared with tar. ﴿It scorches the faces.﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: When the people of the Fire become hungry, they seek relief from the tree of Zaqqum, and they eat from it, and their skins and faces are peeled off, so that if a passerby came who knew them, he would recognize their faces by the skins of their faces in it. Then thirst overtakes them, and they seek relief, and they are given relief with ﴿water like molten brass﴾, which is that whose heat has reached its extreme. When they bring it near their mouths, the flesh of their faces, from which the skin has fallen, is roasted by its heat. ﴿Wretched is the drink, and evil is the Fire as a resting place﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: a dwelling. Mujahid: a gathering place. 'Ata': a place of rest. It was said: a cushion. al-Qutaybi said: a seat. The root of "murtafaq" is a reclining place; it is said of it: "irtafaqtu" when I leaned on a reclining place. The poet said:

"She said to him, and he leaned, 'Ah, is there a youth who drives the people with the gazelles of the forenoon?'" [[Jami' al-Bayan: 15/300.]]

It is also said: "irtafaqa al-rajul," when a man spends the night on his elbow, unable to sleep. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

"The one free of care slept, and I spent the night leaning on my elbow, as if in my eyes is bitter aloe that has been slaughtered." [[Jami' al-Bayan: 15/301; Lisan al-'Arab: 4/397, where it reads "mushtajiran" instead of "murtafiqan."]]

That is, cut off from its support. The "sabb" is a tree which, when uprooted, exudes something like milk, and sometimes a speck rises from it, which falls into the eye, so that it is like a spark of fire, and sometimes weakens the sight. It may also be that His saying "murtafaqan" comes from "rifq," meaning kindness and benefit.

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good work.﴾ His saying "Indeed, We do not waste" is not the predicate of "Indeed, those who believe," but rather a parenthetical statement, and the predicate of the first "inna" (the one at the beginning of the verse) is His saying: ﴿those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾. Similar to this in speech is common; the poet said:

"Indeed the Caliph—indeed God has clothed him with the garment of kingship, by which the endings are hoped for."

Some said: there is an omission in it, for its meaning is: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—then indeed We do not waste their reward but reward them.﴾

Then He mentioned the reward, saying: ﴿those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾, which is an abiding dwelling. ﴿Beneath them rivers will flow﴾. ﴿They will be adorned﴾: they will wear therein ﴿bracelets﴾, which is the plural of "aswar." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: each one of them will be adorned with three bracelets: one of silver, one of gold, and one of pearls and rubies. ﴿of gold﴾. ﴿And they will wear green garments of fine silk﴾, which is what is thin of brocade, ﴿and brocade﴾, which is what is thick of it. It was said: it is a Persian word that has been Arabized. ﴿Reclining therein﴾: in the gardens ﴿on couches﴾, which are thrones in canopies, the singular of which is "arikah." ﴿How excellent the reward, and how good the resting place﴾ — meaning the gardens.

And say not of anything, "I will surely do that tomorrow," without adding, "if God wills." ﴿And say not of anything, "I will surely do that tomorrow," unless God wills.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: this means that when you resolve to do something tomorrow, or swear an oath about something, you should say, "I will do that tomorrow, if God wills." And if you forget the exception and then remember it, say it even after a year. This is a discipline from God to His Prophet (ﷺ), when he was asked about three matters: the People of the Cave, the Spirit, and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he promised to inform them without adding the exception.

'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id al-Maqri narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A servant's faith is not complete until he makes the exception [[i.e., until he says, "If God wills"]] in every statement he makes." [68]

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Hasan said: its meaning is: when you forget the exception and then remember, make the exception. 'Ikrimah said: its meaning is: remember your Lord when you become angry.

'Abd al-Samad ibn Hassan narrated to us, from Wuhayb, who said: It is written in the Gospel: "Son of Adam, remember Me when you are angry, and I will remember you when I am angry, and I will not destroy you among those who are destroyed. And when you are wronged, do not seek vengeance, for My support for you is better than your support for yourself." Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: this refers to the prayer, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever forgets a prayer or sleeps through it, let him pray it when he remembers it." [[Sunan al-Darimi: 1/280.]] [69]

The people of allusion (ahl al-isharah, Sufi interpreters) said: its meaning is ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ other than Him, because the remembrance of God Most High is realized only after forgetting other things. This is supported by the saying of Dhu al-Nun al-Misri: "Whoever remembers God with true remembrance forgets everything in comparison with His remembrance; and when he forgets everything in comparison with His remembrance, God preserves everything for him, and it becomes his substitute for everything." It was also said: its meaning is: remember your Lord when you abandon His remembrance, and forgetting is abandoning.

﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this."﴾ That is, He will keep me on a path nearer to Him, so I will be guided. It was also said: the meaning is, perhaps God will guide and direct me to something nearer than what I promised you and told you would happen, if He wills. It was also said: God commanded him to remember Him whenever he forgets something, and to ask Him to make him remember, so that he recalls, or to guide him to what is better for him than recalling what he forgot.

It is said that when the people asked him about the story of the People of the Cave, out of obstinacy, God commanded him to inform them that God would give him proofs and clear evidence of the truth of his prophethood and of the truth to which he called them, and would guide them to what they asked. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, did so, when He gave him knowledge of the unseen matters of the messengers and their news, which was clearer as proof and closer to right guidance than the story of the People of the Cave. Some of them said: this is something he was commanded to say along with ﴿unless God wills﴾ when he remembers the exception after forgetting it. So when a person forgets, God gives him [[so in the manuscript facsimile]] from that. Its expiation is to say: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this.﴾

﴿And they remained﴾, that is, the People of the Cave, ﴿in their cave﴾. Some said: this is a report about the People of the Scripture, that they said this, and they said: if it were a report from God, Mighty and Majestic, about the exact duration of their stay in the cave, then His saying ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾ would have no understandable sense, and He had already informed His creatures of the length of their stay. This is the view of Qatadah.

It is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And they said: they remained in their cave." Mutar al-Warraq said regarding this verse: this is something the Jews said, and God refuted them, saying: ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained.﴾ Others said: this is God's report about the exact duration of their stay in the cave. They said: the meaning of His saying ﴿Say: God knows best﴾ is that the People of the Scripture said in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "For the youths, from the time they entered the cave until today, is three hundred and nine years." God, Mighty and Majestic, refuted that, saying: ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾ after He took their souls, until today. None knows that except God and whomever God has informed of it. Al-Kalbi said: the Christians of Najran said: "As for the three hundred, we know it, but as for the nine, we have no knowledge of them," so it was revealed: ﴿God knows best how long they remained.﴾

"Three hundred years" in the genitive construction without tanwin, was recited by Hamzah and al-Kisa'i; the others recite it with tanwin, meaning: and they remained in their cave three hundred years. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: the revelation came ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred [years]﴾ and they said: "Days or years?" So it was revealed, "years" (sinin), and therefore He said "years" and did not say "year." ﴿And they added nine.﴾ ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained. His is the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears!﴾ That means: how much God sees everything that exists! And how much He hears everything that is heard! ﴿They have no protector besides Him﴾, that is, the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth have no protector apart from God, ﴿no helper﴾: a supporter. ﴿And He does not share His command with anyone﴾, [meaning] among the idols or others.

﴿And recite﴾, that is, read, O Muhammad, ﴿what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾, meaning: the Qur'an, and follow what is in it. ﴿None can alter His words﴾. Al-Kalbi said: none can change the Qur'an. Muhammad ibn Jarir said: that is, none can change what He has threatened with His words against the people of disobedience and those who oppose His Book. ﴿And you will never find, other than Him, a refuge﴾, if you do not follow the Qur'an and oppose it. Ibn 'Abbas said: a shelter. al-Hasan said: a place of entry. It was said: a place of deviation. It was said: a refuge. Mujahid said: a shelter; its root is from inclining, and from it comes the word "lahd" (the niche of a grave).

﴿And restrain yourself﴾ – the verse –

The exegetes said: it was revealed concerning 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari, because he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) before this verse was revealed, and with him were Bilal, Suhayb, Khabbab, 'Ammar, 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Mihja' and Salman. Salman was wearing a cloak in which he had been sweating, and in his hand was a palm frond which he was splitting and weaving. 'Uyaynah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Does the smell of these people not bother you? By God, their smell has harmed us." He said: "We are the masters and nobles of Mudar. If we embrace Islam, the people will embrace Islam; and if we refuse, the people will refuse. Nothing prevents us from following you except these people. So remove them, until we follow you, and make for us a gathering and for them a gathering."

Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And restrain yourself﴾, that is, hold yourself ﴿with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾: who worship their Lord and honor Him, ﴿seeking His face﴾, that is, seeking God, Mighty and Majestic, not seeking any worldly gain. What is meant is good deeds and abandoning showing off. Qatadah said: that means the dawn and afternoon prayers. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: By Him in whose hand my soul is, they are the people of the obligatory prayers. Qatadah said: this verse was revealed concerning the People of the Suffah, who were seven hundred poor men who kept to the mosque of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), not returning to trade, nor to crops, nor to livestock; they would pray one prayer and wait for another.

Qatadah said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "Praise be to God who has placed in my community those with whom I was commanded to be patient." [[Musnad Abi Ya'la: 2/383.]] [70]

﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾: do not turn your eyes away from them toward others, ﴿desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾, meaning sitting with the leaders, the rich, and the nobles.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾, desiring worldly adornment, while they are immersed in seeking forgiveness, because that would be a judgment against the Prophet (ﷺ) for desiring this world. ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾, that is, whose heart We left and made forget Our remembrance. Abu al-'Aliyah said: this means Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. Others said: it means 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn. ﴿And he followed his desire, and his affair was [ever] neglect﴾. Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: lost. Dawud said: regret. Habbab said: destruction. Ibn Zayd said: opposing the truth. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: excess. al-Akhfash said: exceeding the limit. al-Farra' said: abandoned. It was said: vain. Abu Zayd al-Balkhi said: going ahead in evil. Abu 'Ubayd said: it comes from the saying of the Arabs: "a horse, a fars-fart," when it outruns the other horses; and "the word of mine was farat," meaning it preceded. It was also said: its meaning is that he wasted his affair and left his days idle. They said: the believer is one who uses his time, and time does not use him.

﴿And say: the truth is from your Lord﴾. "The truth" is nominative as a quotation (hikayah). It was also said it is nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "And say: it is the truth from your Lord," that is, what was mentioned of the Qur'an, faith, and the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said it is nominative as the subject, with its predicate being "from your Lord." The meaning of the verse: Say, O Muhammad, to those whose hearts We made heedless of Our remembrance: O people, the truth is from your Lord, and to Him belongs success and abandonment, and in His hand is misguidance and guidance; He guides whom He wills to believe, and misguides whom He wills to disbelieve. [[In the Isfahan copy: "then let him disbelieve." (Marginal note of the Isfahan copy.)]] Nothing of that is up to me. I am not driving away the believers for your sake. If you wish, believe; and if you wish, disbelieve. For if you disbelieve, your Lord has prepared for your disbelief a fire whose enclosure surrounds you; and if you believe and obey, then for you is what God, Mighty and Majestic, has described for the people of His obedience.

His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ is not a permission or choice; rather it is a warning and threat, like His saying: ﴿Do what you will.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever God wills faith for, believes, and whoever God wills disbelief for, disbelieves. This is His saying: ﴿And you do not will, except that God wills.﴾

﴿Indeed, We have prepared﴾: We prepared and made ready, from "al-'utad," which is equipment. ﴿For the wrongdoers﴾: for the disbelievers, ﴿a Fire﴾. In it is evidence that the Fire is created, for if it were not created and existing and prepared, the one who informed would be a liar, and God is exalted above that.

His saying: ﴿Its enclosure surrounds them﴾.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The enclosure of the Fire is four walls, thick, each one a distance of forty years." [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 15/298.]] [71]

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a wall of fire.

Al-Kalbi said: it is a neck that comes out of the Fire and encircles the disbelievers like an enclosure. Al-Qutaybi said: the "saradiq" is the chamber that surrounds the tent. Ru'bah said:

"O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud... the enclosure of glory is extended over you."

Salamah ibn Jandal said:

"He is the one who admitted al-Nu'man into a house whose roof is... the chests of elephants, after a tent that is enclosed."

Here it means the smoke that will surround the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, which God mentioned in Surat al-Mursalat: ﴿Proceed to a shadow of three branches.﴾ [[Surat al-Mursalat: 30.]]

﴿And if they seek relief﴾ from the intensity of thirst, ﴿they will be given relief with water like molten brass﴾.

Abu Muslim narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding ﴿water like molten brass﴾, he said: "Like the dregs of oil; when it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off into it." [[Musnad Ahmad: 3/71.]] [72] Ibn 'Abbas said: thick water like the sediment of oil. al-A'mash said: it is the residue of oil. Mujahid said: pus and blood. al-Dahhak said: al-muhl is black water, and Hell is black, its water is black, its trees are black, and its people are black. Abu 'Ubaydah said: everything that is melted from the substances of the earth.

Rawh ibn 'Ubadah narrated from Sa'id, from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that a vessel of gold and silver was presented to Ibn Mas'ud. He ordered a trench to be dug in the ground, then fuel of good firewood was thrown in, then that vessel was thrown into it. When it foamed and melted, he said to his servant: "Call whoever is present from the people of Kufa." He called a group, and when they entered upon him, he said: "Do you see this?" They said: "Yes." He said: "We have never seen in this world anything more similar to al-muhl than this gold and silver when it foamed and melted." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: al-muhl is that whose heat has reached its extreme.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: I heard al-Muntaji' ibn Nabhan mention a man, and he said: "He is more hateful to me than al-tulya and al-muhl." I said to him: "What is al-muhl?" He said: "It is a crust that is cut from the sides of the bread by fire, bright red, very red, as if it were a pomegranate; it is a live coal." Al-tulya: the she-camel smeared with tar. ﴿It scorches the faces.﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: When the people of the Fire become hungry, they seek relief from the tree of Zaqqum, and they eat from it, and their skins and faces are peeled off, so that if a passerby came who knew them, he would recognize their faces by the skins of their faces in it. Then thirst overtakes them, and they seek relief, and they are given relief with ﴿water like molten brass﴾, which is that whose heat has reached its extreme. When they bring it near their mouths, the flesh of their faces, from which the skin has fallen, is roasted by its heat. ﴿Wretched is the drink, and evil is the Fire as a resting place﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: a dwelling. Mujahid: a gathering place. 'Ata': a place of rest. It was said: a cushion. al-Qutaybi said: a seat. The root of "murtafaq" is a reclining place; it is said of it: "irtafaqtu" when I leaned on a reclining place. The poet said:

"She said to him, and he leaned, 'Ah, is there a youth who drives the people with the gazelles of the forenoon?'" [[Jami' al-Bayan: 15/300.]]

It is also said: "irtafaqa al-rajul," when a man spends the night on his elbow, unable to sleep. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

"The one free of care slept, and I spent the night leaning on my elbow, as if in my eyes is bitter aloe that has been slaughtered." [[Jami' al-Bayan: 15/301; Lisan al-'Arab: 4/397, where it reads "mushtajiran" instead of "murtafiqan."]]

That is, cut off from its support. The "sabb" is a tree which, when uprooted, exudes something like milk, and sometimes a speck rises from it, which falls into the eye, so that it is like a spark of fire, and sometimes weakens the sight. It may also be that His saying "murtafaqan" comes from "rifq," meaning kindness and benefit.

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not waste the reward of one who does good work.﴾ His saying "Indeed, We do not waste" is not the predicate of "Indeed, those who believe," but rather a parenthetical statement, and the predicate of the first "inna" (the one at the beginning of the verse) is His saying: ﴿those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾. Similar to this in speech is common; the poet said:

"Indeed the Caliph—indeed God has clothed him with the garment of kingship, by which the endings are hoped for."

Some said: there is an omission in it, for its meaning is: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—then indeed We do not waste their reward but reward them.﴾

Then He mentioned the reward, saying: ﴿those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾, which is an abiding dwelling. ﴿Beneath them rivers will flow﴾. ﴿They will be adorned﴾: they will wear therein ﴿bracelets﴾, which is the plural of "aswar." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: each one of them will be adorned with three bracelets: one of silver, one of gold, and one of pearls and rubies. ﴿of gold﴾. ﴿And they will wear green garments of fine silk﴾, which is what is thin of brocade, ﴿and brocade﴾, which is what is thick of it. It was said: it is a Persian word that has been Arabized. ﴿Reclining therein﴾: in the gardens ﴿on couches﴾, which are thrones in canopies, the singular of which is "arikah." ﴿How excellent the reward, and how good the resting place﴾ — meaning the gardens.

And say not of anything, "I will surely do that tomorrow," without adding, "if God wills." ﴿And say not of anything, "I will surely do that tomorrow," unless God wills.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: this means that when you resolve to do something tomorrow, or swear an oath about something, you should say, "I will do that tomorrow, if God wills." And if you forget the exception and then remember it, say it even after a year. This is a discipline from God to His Prophet (ﷺ), when he was asked about three matters: the People of the Cave, the Spirit, and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he promised to inform them without adding the exception.
